And whereas the development of a national capital is at least in part a national responsibility;
And whereas the capital of Canada is designated by the British North America Act to be Ottawa;

And whereas the carrying out of planned improvements requires a clear expression of intention to proceed with necessary developments in a manner which will ensure continuity; Therefore this house is of opinion:

column2: That it is desirable that all developments of the capital should be in accordance 'with an approved plan which has regard to the position of the city of Ottawa as a national capital in the present, and to its probable needs as the capital of Canada in years to come.

That a special account in the consolidated revenue fund, to be known as the national capital fund, should be created to which appropriation may be made annually by parliament over a period of years of the amounts required from time to time to meet the costs of such projects as may lie recommended by the federal district commission and approved by the governor in

column1: Development of National Capital
council for the development of the national capital and the surrounding area, in accordance with the plan;

column2: That it is desirable that the work necessary to this end be under the supervision of the federal district commission, distinct from its ordinary operations;
That the expenditure of moneys for these purposes should be conditional on the effective co-operation of the city of Ottawa and other municipalities within the national capital district.

column1: He said: I know hon. members are anxious that the session should be concluded with as little delay as possible; therefore I promise I shall not take up much time with this resolution. I believe the resolution in the form in which it appears on the order paper will commend itself to hon. members without extended discussion. Most of the objectives set forth have been approved in past years, and the general conception I believe has met with acceptance not only in parliament but throughout the country.

As hon. members know, there are items in t'be estimates in relation to the work of the federal district commission. For that reason I shall not in my present remarks go into detail about specific projects. Questions on that particular phase of the matter may be asked when we reach those estimates.

The resolution, in a word, seeks to ensure the continuous development of Ottawa and surrounding areas in a manner which will help to meet its needs as the capital of Canada both at the present time and in years to come. I would link together, as setting forth the essentials of the resolution, certain clauses which appear in it. For this purpose I shall quote from the resolution, but in an order different from that in which these clauses appear.
The resolution states:

That it is desirable that all developments of the capital should be in accordance with an approved plan which has regard to the position of the city of Ottawa as a national capital in the present, and to its probable needs as the capital of Canada in years to come.
The requirements of a national capital involve from time to time developments of a character beyond the municipal improvements ordinarily required in other cities.
The carrying out of planned improvements requires a clear expression of intention to proceed with necessary developments in a manner which will ensure continuity.

A special account in the consolidated revenue fund, to be knowm as the national capital fund, should be created, to which appropriation may be made annually by parliament over a period of years of the amounts required from time to time to meet the costs of such projects as may be recommended by the federal district commission and approved by the governor in council
for the development of the national capital and the surrounding area, in accordance with the plan.
I believe those four paragraphs, which I have rearranged in this order, will give to hon. members the essentials of the resolution.
May I now for a moment enlarge upon the statements therein set forth. It is 6tated first that-

It is desirable that all developments of the capital should be in accordance with an approved plan which has regard to the position of the city of Ottawa as a national capital in the present, and to its probable needs as the capital of Canada in years to come.

What was known as the Ottawa improvement commission was appointed during the administration of Sir Wilfrid Laurier within one year of fifty"" years ago in order, as a federal government responsibility, to assist in, making in this city such necessary improvements as at that time seemed advisable, having regard to the fact that Ottawa was the capital of Canada. Those improvements have continued over the years, and hon. members now know the effect they have had upon Ottawa as the capital city of our country.

I need not go into details as to what has been accomplished over those years; the vast improvements, so apparent on all sides, speak for themselves. I would ask hon. members, however, to ask themselves what would have been the position in this capital today if those improvements had not been made during the last fifty years. It is in this light that I now present to the house this resolution, one which I hope will lead to essential developments which the city of Ottawa could not be expected to undertake as a municipal obligation, if the capital is to meet the needs which will be expected of it in the course of another fifty years, to say nothing of the years which will follow thereafter.

Unless these essential developments are made at the present time they will be extremely costly to make within another few years, if indeed it might not become next to impossible to make them later on. It is to anticipate a situation of that kind that I am bringing forward this resolution today.

As hon. members are aware, for some years past members of the federal district commission and others who are members of the capital planning committee, including several experts, have been working on a plan for the development of the capital. A master plan is being prepared setting out on broad lines the developments which should be followed from
Development oj National Capital

year to year by the different authorities and organizations having to do with the development of the capital. Here may I 'point, out that the municipality of Ottawa has its obliga-gations; the provinces of Ontario and Quebec each have also to do with matters which pertain to Ottawa and Hull and which affect the development of the capital. .Adjoining municipalities have to be brought into consideration in connection with developments affecting their areas. Finally in association with these authorities there are developments which the government itself, which has a special responsibility for the development of the national capital, will wish to make.

These several bodies cannot be brought together in harmonious relationship unless *there is some broad and general plan to be followed. For that reason, for some years past the government, as I haive said, has had experts at work under the direction of the federal district commission, preparing a master plan; in that work it has had the benefit of the best advice obtainable.

1541988,ca.proc.d.1948-06-28.2.5.1.5,1948-06-28,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Mr. MACKENZIE KING:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council,QUESTIONS,NATIONAL CAPITAL,DEVELOPMENT UNDER APPROVED PLAN-PROVISION FOR ANNUAL APPROPRIATIONS,May I ask that I be permitted to continue my general statement? If there are details which I have not covered, they might be brought up for discussion on the estimates relating to the commission. At that time I would be happy so far as possible to answer any questions which may be asked.

The question the hon. member has just asked respecting an approved plan is one which I was about immediately to anticipate. I do not think the words ""approved plan"" should be taken as meaning that any plan prepared at the moment is to be followed in all details over the next twenty, forty, fifty or a hundred years or that any plan should be approved as a whole by the government or by parliament; but rather that developments should be made in stages in accordance with general ideas which seem to meet with general acceptance and which are in the nature of guides to the future.

A tentative plan is in the making, but it is not completed. As prepared, it deals with general features of the development of the city, including, for example, the main thoroughfares which should be developed; what should be done with railway tracks which intersect different parts of the city; where certain public buildings may be best located, and the like. That plan has already reached the stage which I believe would enable anyone looking at it to see exactly the lines of contemplated future developments. As agreement is reached among the different agencies or governments affected, it would be possible to have developments arranged upon those lines. I do not think however that too much significance should be attached to the word ""approved"" before the word ""plan,"" as related to the plan as a whole, or as 'to finality in its details. This is true particularly in view of the fact that no further stage in the development planned on a large scale can take place without parliament approving in the first instance the essential projects being proposed.

The conception of following a master plan is I think imperative if development is to take place in an orderly way, and in a manner which will admit of projects once begun being carried out with a degree of certainty from year to year, different stages, as I have said, being approved by parliament from year to year as the years go by.
I attach great importance to the following statement:
The requirements of a national capital involve, from time to time, developments of a character beyond the municipal improvements ordinarily required in other cities.

That is why the government is asking today that this House of Commons declare its readiness to support the progress toward completion of certain developments which, once approved by parliament, may in the very nature of things not be possible of completion all at once and which may require appropriations from time to time over a series of years. Already the city of Ottawa, the government of Ontario, the government of Quebec, some of the municipalities adjoining Ottawa, and the federal district commission, have been in communication with each other with respect to certain developments which they all feel to be more or less essential and which they would like to see commenced at once. These are developments that could not be expected from the municipality itself; they are developments that might not be made if Ottawa were not the capital of our country and there were not necessarily regard for the future development of the country as well as of the municipality.
Development oj National Capital

These various authorities wish to have some assurance that if a certain development is undertaken it will be proceeded with, that it will not be started this year by an appropriation by parliament of a certain amount and then dropped in the year following. They are asking that this parliament indicate, first, its belief in following a plan, and, second, its intention to see that essential developments under that plan are presented to parliament from time to time and developed along lines which may continue to receive the approval of parliament.

Perhaps 1 could not do better at the moment than to anticipate what might be asked with respect to the immediate developments the federal district commission have in mind and that the government is recommending in connection with an item that appears in the supplementary estimates at this time. Before giving that in detail it might help to disclose the importance of the proposed developments were I to say a word about the appearance of this capital as I recall it before some of the major developments in the capital, because of its being the capital, were made at the instance of the government.

We hear a great deal of complaint about traffic congestion and confusion in the centre of the city, between the houses of parliament, the Chateau Laurier and the station, and particularly around the national war memorial. I remember well what the city was like before the changes were made that have since produced such a splendid effect.

When a Liberal administration came into office in the early twenties the spape now occupied by the national war memorial and the open spaces immediately adjoining were occupied by a block of buildings, including a hotel; by a second hotel, a post office, a theatre, a city hall and a church-all in that limited space. In the space which the national war memorial now occupies there was a mass of buildings between Elgin street and a point close to the approaches to the Chateau Laurier, and again between Wellington and Sparks streets. There was one side of a hotel on the corner opposite the Langevin block; there were other shops and stores that ran on down Elgin street from Wellington to Sparks street; there was a series of shops and stores along Sparks street; on Wellington street, there were offices and shops and another side of the hotel. Behind that block was the Ottawa post office, which occupied a considerable space. Today it is located on the corner of Elgin and Sparks street.

On the far side of Sparks street opposite this commercial block was the largest hotel in the city, the Russell hotel, with shops and stores adjoining. Behind and adjoining the Russell hotel was a large theatre. Beyond the Russell hotel and the theatre was the city hall and Knox church. Along Elgin street there was a row of dwellings which, had they not been removed, would now be standing on the east side, making that street half the width it is at the present time.

All the improvements I have mentioned have been made within the last fifteen or twenty years, and in accordance with a plan agreed to by the government and the municipality, each sharing in the cost. They have changed entirely the appearance of the city and have given some breathing space in this central part of the capital.

Congestion due to the growth of the city and from other causes is again taking place in this area. Traffic of larger proportions and of a different kind is now being found on the streets in the very heart of the city. Twenty years ago we had not the enormous trucks and vans which are now making use of any thoroughfare they find most convenient. They are making their presence all too greatly felt in this area, an area in which they would scarcely have been able to operate had it not undergone so much in the way of improvement. The commission, the city authorities and others have come to 'the conclusion that a major development is necessary if this congestion is to be relieved. The traffic of heavier vehicles must be directed away from in front of the parliament, buildings and the centre of the city to some other portion.

It is proposed that a bridge should be thrown across the canal south of the station to run from Elgin street to Waller street. It would cross at a point half way between Sparks street, where the monument is situated, and the Laurier avenue bridge. Last year the house approved appropriations which enabled soundings and other investigations to be made respecting the feasibility of constructing a bridge there. The reports are favourable, and the commission is asking, in the appropriation which parliament will be requested to vote later, for money to enable it to proceed with the immediate construction of that bridge. It may take considerable time to complete, but when completed it will have the effect of removing heavy truck and other traffic from this part of the city to another more suitable part.
Development of National Capital

Another major improvement that is desired is in relation to the location of railroad tracks and freight terminals. I ask hon. members to contemplate what the situation will be like twenty or fifty years hence if the freight terminals which are now located where they are in this capital are allowed to remain without any anticipation of the growth of traffic, on the one hand, and the growth of the city and its needs, to say nothing of the country, on the other. Within a quarter mile of these houses of parliament one can see, from the very windows of this building, freight terminals in the immediate vicinity of the Union station. Going toward government house in the near vicinity of the research council building and Earnscliffe one can see on the other side of the street, facing the Ottawa river, freight terminals which are occupying space which should be reserved for public buildings of first importance to the country.

The commission and the city both feel that some arrangements should be made with the railroad companies to have these freight terminals placed in another part of the city. That will not be accomplished in a day, and it will not be accomplished by any one authority. It can only be brought about by the co-operation of the different interests concerned, but a beginning is necessary if the change is ever to be made. What the government has already done to anticipate that end has been to ask parliament to approve first the expenditure of a certain amount of money for the acquisition of lands in those parts of the city which appear likely, in accordance with the general plan, to provide suitable locations, and to appropriate money for the approaches in order that the terminals may be placed in parts that would be appropriate. In other words, what the commission has had in mind is providing zoning areas, which will have regard to what should be reserved for governmental purposes, for commercial purposes, and for residential purposes, and to enter on this task at once while there is opportunity, to have these needs planned and that without too much in the way of expense.

The commission have asked that they should have the right to take up with the railway companies some of the major changes to which I have referred. I have had conversations with the president and chairman of the Canadian Pacific Railway and with the president of the Canadian National Railways, and these gentlemen have expressed their entire sympathy with the development of

the capital of Canada in accordance with a general plan. They would wish however to have considered very carefully any change that would have to be made and the time at which it is to be made. They recognize that some changes will be necessary in the course of time, and they are prepared to co-operate with the commission in seeking to work out a plan which will permit of that development in the most satisfactory way.

I should like to mention one or two other contemplated developments, but that would take up time that cannot be spared at the moment. What I have sought to do today is to make clear to the house the main purpose of the resolution: first, to have it known as the desire of the house that in necessary developments in the capital we should follow a plan; and second, to have the assurance from parliament that when these developments are begun the authorities may have reason to feel that they will be continued in accordance with provision made by parliament from year to year in such amounts as it may deem appropriate. Here let me again make clear that there is no likelihood of a major development taking place which will not be fully under the control of parliament. In the first instance recommendations will be made by the federal district commission in accordance with the advice of their experts and after consultation with the other interests affected. The projects recommended will then have to be approved, first, by order in council of the government so that great care may be taken at that stage, and in the second place by the appropriation of the necessary moneys for these projects by parliament. Lastly, appropriations will be made from year to year, so that parliament may have very full control where federal expenditures are involved.

Another way to have proceeded might have been to ask parliament to vote a large amount of money as was done in the case of the development of Washington, the development of Paris, and other cities, so that the commission, with that guarantee, could have looked forward to a series of developments being effected without interruption over the years. The government felt, however, it rvould be preferable, while having an assurance from parliament of its intention to have the developments proceeded with continuously, to reserve to parliament the control which it would have from year to year of the necessary outlays for all these developments.

I should like to emphasize to hon. members how the whole position of the capital has altered within very recent years. I remember when I first came into office there was not a foreign mission in this country, nor did we
Development oj National Capital

have a single mission representing Canada in a foreign country. We had no representatives in Canada from any of the other dominions, nor from the United Kingdom. We had one representative of our own in the person of the high commissioner in London, and we had a representative of Canada in Paris, but apart from those two representatives of the government there were no representatives here from the governments of the United Kingdom or the other dominions and none from the heads of foreign states. There were no legations and no embassies. There are now something like twenty-five different missions established right here in this capital. The representatives of various countries require accommodation in the city, and more will be coming.

Further may I point out how the capital has increasingly become the centre for important conventions, of conferences, dominion conferences, commonwealth conferences, international conferences, and the like. We have had one visit to our capital from Their Majesties the King and Queen. I think we may look forward to the day when the king and queen will reside for part of the year in the capital of Canada. I am saying nothing at the moment about such matters as tourist traffic, and the importance to Canada of what has been done by its capital to attract visitors to our country. As all hon. members know, the capital of a country is a centre of attraction, and we must look forward to the development of Ottawa in the light of that larger vision. Moreover, the public buildings and public thoroughfares of a capital should lend inspiration to its position as a centre of the culture of the nation, its arts, letters, science and government. Countries are more or less known by their capitals.

When one speaks of other countries, of France, for instance, one thinks of Paris and how beautifully it is laid out; when we speak of Italy, we think of Rome; when we speak of the United Kingdom, we think of London; when we speak of the United States, we think of Washington; indeed, when we think of Greece and Italy, even as they were in ancient times, we are still able to see how Athens and Rome were planned centuries ago.

I believe, as I think all hon. members of this house believe, that Canada may have a future greater than that of almost any of the countries I have mentioned. The day will come, I believe, when this dominion will hold first place among the nations of the British commonwealth. The United Kingdom will always be its spiritual centre, if you wish to use that expression, but even today this Dominion of Canada is the most fortunate country in the world. It has possibilities of development which no other country begins to possess. The proposal which the government is bringing

forward today in the form of a resolution has been framed with a view to helping to meet the needs of Canada's capital in the present. It also, and even more, seeks to anticipate the needs of Canada's capital in the future as we believe that future will shape our country. We desire a capital adequate at all times to the country's needs. We desire, above all else, a capital worthy of the high place that Canada holds in the world today and of the Canada that is yet to be.

RUSSELL BOUCHER (Carleton):,,QUESTIONS,NATIONAL CAPITAL,DEVELOPMENT UNDER APPROVED PLAN-PROVISION FOR ANNUAL APPROPRIATIONS,Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the members of this house agree with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in what he has said as to the development of Ottawa as the national capital.

I was pleased to hear him emphasize in his closing words that Ottawa, as the capital of Canada, is becoming more and more a mecca for important conventions and conferences and a host of tourists. His suggestion that at some future time royalty itself may spend considerable time in Ottawa will have a bearing on the way in which the Canadian people and members of the House of Commons look on this resolution.

I had hoped that time would have permitted the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to give more details on the development of the capital so far. We know that for approximately fifty years the House of Commons has considered the development of a national capital area. Many attempts, plans and projects have been put before the people of the dominion and of the city in regard to the development of the national capital. As the representative of an area within the city of Ottawa, I think it is proper that I should draw the attention of the house to the fact that Ottawa is faced with a problem in her desire to co-operate with the dominion in forming a national capital worthy of the great nation that we believe Canada will be. She has also had grave difficulties in the development of her own internal management because of her desire to work on a general master plan and co-operate in every way she can in the development of a capital area.

I emphasize the Prime Minister's statement that everything cannot be shown on a master plan; but it is important that the people of this area, and the people of Canada as a whole, should have some assurance that many projects will be proceeded with which are necessary to the economy of Ottawa. Because of Ottawa's beautiful location she has an industrial potentiality which would be an important factor if Ottawa were developed as an industrial city rather than a capital area. Because Ottawa has given up her opportunities of developing as an industrial city in favour of
Development of National Capital

a federal area, hon. members should appreciate the difficulties which confront the people of Ottawa in planning their future development. Because of that I should like to see this resolution go much further than it does.

The Prime Minister mentioned the development around confederation square which has taken place within the last twenty years. I need not remind hon. members or anybody else of the beauty of Elgin street and confederation square. That is obvious to anybody who visits Ottawa. But also obvious to those who appreciate the beauty of it is the adverse effect it has on traffic. I emphasize the necessity of keeping that point in mind. I was pleased to hear the Prime Minister say that the immediate project he had in mind was the construction of a bridge from Elgin street to Waller street, which will relieve traffic congestion in the bottleneck around confederation square. Hon. members will find that everybody in Ottawa, and everybody having anything to do with Ottawa, realizes that that is one of the most important projects that could be undertaken at the earliest opportunity. To undertake that requires not only federal government assistance in the way of the use of federal property in the development of the national capital, but also the co-operation of the railways, transportation facilities and various services in the city itself. Coupled with that is the cross-town track situation which I am sure every hon. member knows has had a detrimental effect on the development of Ottawa. Therefore these two projects need immediate attention.

A number of reports have been made on future projects for the development of the national capital. All have had a bearing on the development of Ottawa. The Prime Minister mentioned the expropriation of land which is taking place under the aegis of the federal district commission. These reports visualize removing our terminals and establishing manufacturing and commercial areas or industrial areas. The development of Ottawa from the point of view of expansion is in a critical stage because the city has not expanded her boundaries. Municipalities adjacent to the city have become inundated with new developments. That situation also aas some bearing on how Ottawa will develop jn the future, whether it will be through the oorough system, government services, or through some other system.

I think the city will willingly accept a certain degree of leadership from the dominion government in the development of the capital area. The city of Ottawa would appreciate a lead from hon. members and parliament as

a whole in the development of the capital area before the city undertakes the immediately urgent problems confronting it within its own economy. The city of Ottawa cannot proceed with the necessary and immediate developments without giving every regard possible to the capital area development and without co-operating with the federal district commission.

I had hoped that in introducing this resolution the Prime Minister would take the House of Commons more into his confidence and give us more details. I was particularly anxious to see him ask for the co-operation of hon. members outside of Ottawa and of the provinces in developing the capital area.

On a previous occasion I recommended that within the federal area certain areas should be set aside for provincial show rooms or show places. I believe that the large acreage which is being set aside or designated as a capital area could very well be used to the advantage of this nation and to the interest of the provinces. Within that area certain areas should be set aside to be developed by the provinces and administered to their own advantage. Each province could use these sites to show its own industries and its own beauty. On that occasion I suggested that the federal district commission driveway should be extended from the city in a northwesterly direction to Fitzroy Harbour, in Ontario, and thence on the Quebec side of the river back to Ottawa. Along this highway certain acreages of land could be set aside for each of the provinces to develop as provincial showrooms, thus making the whole capital area scheme a truly national scheme in which every province would feel it had a little bit. of home to develop in the federal area.

I do hope that the Prime Minister and the federal district commission will develop this idea, because one of the greatest detriments to the development of the capital area is the feeling that it is a development purely for the city of Ottawa. That feeling is not in accordance with the facts. While Ottawa will benefit because of her strategic location and because the capital of the country is located within her boundaries, she has something to offer to the federal area which no other place in Canada has. But she has also to develop her own economy commensurate with the wishes of the nation at large. If you go to Montreal, Toronto or any other large Canadian city you will see that the dominion government and the railways have established government buildings, postal terminals, railway centres, union terminals and so on. When you see that you realize the amount of money that has been spent in each of these cities
Development oj National Capital

purely for railway and transportation facilities, for the city itself. Ottawa has had that for some years. But this city, from the standpoint of railways, has much more, to consider, because of the presence here of the parliament buildings, than any other city in Canada. I feel therefore that in supporting this resolution hon. members should take the view that in establishing a capital area in this city and its environs they are establishing a little bit of their own home and advertising their own nation in a special way.

I do not quite know what the resolution means when it predicates this scheme upon the co-operation of the municipalities with the dominion. I do not understand why the resolution fails to make any reference to co-operation on the part of the two provinces concerned. I do not see in the resolution anything pointing to the expectation of co-operation from the provinces. I would point out that the federal area extends into the province of Quebec. Each of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec has of course its own legislature, and the respective municipalities are jealous of their own authority. The municipalities themselves feel that they should have some say, some interest, in the development of the capital area to the extent that such development affects their communities. I hope therefore that the omission from the resolution of any reference to co-operation on the part of the provinces is purely an oversight and is not to be taken as implying that the dominion government will proceed without the utmost co-operation from these provinces.

I shall not go into the matter at any great length now. I think it would be better to wait until the estimates are before us. I thought it might be well, however, to mention these few points at this stage in the hope that the Prime Minister, when the estimates are under consideration, will be prepared to give to the house such information as is necessary to a proper understanding of the proposal we have before us.

COLDWELL (Rosetown-Biggar):,,QUESTIONS,NATIONAL CAPITAL,DEVELOPMENT UNDER APPROVED PLAN-PROVISION FOR ANNUAL APPROPRIATIONS,Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a few words on this subject, both as one who is now living in Ottawa and as one who is interested in Canada's capital apart from the fact of his residence here.

Ottawa is probably one of the most beautiful sites that any capital in the world enjoys. With the background of the river and the Gatineau hills, with the beautiful countryside surrounding the city, it is indeed a fine setting for a capital, and I have often regretted that the plans which have now been formulated and are now before us for discussionthe plans formulated during the prime ministership of my right hon. friend-were not thought of many years ago. The city itself is not well laid out. There is congestion in the narrow streets, and if streetcars are not replaced by a more modern transportation system such as buses or trolley buses, the congestion will continue and the city will be cluttered up with the present antiquated conveyances.

I hope the municipality will realize that it too has an obligation in connection with the beautification of this most attractive city. I may add, however, that before we spend very large sums of money on the beautification of the capital, seeing that it has been neglected for so many years and was not conceived in the manner in which I think it should have been conceived, we should bear in mind the importance of putting first things first.

If I may use the slang expression, we do not want a country or a capital with a Queen Anne front and a Mary Anne back. We should try to avoid any suggestion of that sort in connection with our capital or with the country as a whole. When we are talking about the beautification of Ottawa we should remember that there are certain projects, apart from the beautification of the capital, that ought to be kept clearly in our minds.

I am thinking of a trans-Canada highway that would be a credit to this country and to our people, a highway that would attract visitors to our beautiful countryside. Our roads across Canada are to a large extent disgraceful and impassable, and no province can undertake the building of the kind of trans-Canada highway which is needed. Someone says, come to Saskatchewan and travel on the trans-Canada highway. Yes. I agree that a province which has thirty-eight per cent of the roads in the dominion cannot possibly undertake the building of the kind of trans-Canada highway which is necessary in order to give proper service. Thirty-eight, per cent of the roads in Canada are located in Saskatchewan-and I am using this government's statistics, not those of the provincial government.

There is at the present time in western Canada the possibility of a serious crop failure in many parts of the prairies owing to the drought. Again, we have to consider the economy of the country, upon which expenditures for the beautification of the capital must rest.

1542029,ca.proc.d.1948-06-28.2.5.1.46,1948-06-28,a990e2af-c044-40da-880c-510347167930,ca.m.4348,Mr. J. T. RICHARD (Ottawa East):,,QUESTIONS,NATIONAL CAPITAL,DEVELOPMENT UNDER APPROVED PLAN-PROVISION FOR ANNUAL APPROPRIATIONS,Mr. Speaker, I do not believe anyone could speak on this resolution without first paying tribute to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for having given so much of his time, energy and ability to the formulation of plans, with the assistance of experts, which will make Ottawa and the area surrounding it a national capital worthy of this country.

I am sure all hon. members will agree that any request for money for the implementation of the plans for a national capital area should be approved. But we should understand also that any criticism offered in this regard is brought forward in order to assist, and to express the honest point of view of members from different parts of the country. I believe we all agree on the general plan for the improvement of the city of Ottawa. I do regret, however, as I have said on other occasions, that members of this house-including mysel f, and I was born here and have lived in Ottawa all my life-do not know enough about that general plan or the details concerning the improvement of the capital area. I suggest that at the next session we set up a committee of this house, or perhaps a joint committee of this house and the senate, which could be apprised of the specific details the federal district commission has in mind for the improvement of this area. If hon. members knew a little more about these matters I believe it would be much easier to get approval of the necessary expenditures, and in addition those who are formulating the plans would have the benefit of the viewpoint of those coming from other parts of the country, so that this could be made a truly national plan.

Speaking as a citizen of Ottawa, and representing one of its constituencies, while criticism is sometimes levelled at the city itself I must remind hon. members that at times it is not very pleasant for the people of this city to find that they do not know exactly where they are going or what they are to do. In this connection I would mention the matter of expropriation. Perhaps very few hon. members
Development oj National Capital

realize that the federal district commission suddenly files a plan in the registry office under which a certain area, which has been a residential area, at once becomes the property of the crown. A good deal of property has been expropriated in this way, and no doubt more will be expropriated; and the people living in these houses want to know where they are to go. All along the Rideau and Ottawa rivers new houses have been expropriated. The people will not receive their money for perhaps five years. In the meantime they have been told that they may remain for perhaps two years, but that then they must find somewhere else to live. They have no place to go. Under the general plan it is true that certain areas have been set aside as residential areas, but they do not have the necessary services; and the city of Ottawa cannot even furnish services for the municipalities which may be annexed in the near future. Much less are we able to provide the water and other necessary services which will be required if all these people are to be moved within the next few years. That is why I should like some assurance that the-e people will not be required to leave their present homes until the federal district commission has provided other areas within the city where houses can be built and where they will have the transportation, water, and other essential services they have enjoyed in the past.

I would remind lion, members that the lot of the Ottawa people is not as easy as they imagine. When people have resided for many years in an area which is close to their work and then they are told that within a few years -we do not know when-they must either build a house or rent one from someone else who will build one, the situation becomes very difficult for them. Perhaps that might answer what is said at times, and I have no doubt honestly, by the leader of the CiC.F., that the municipality might be responsible for certain conditions in housing. We do not know where we are going.

I am not blaming the master plan itself; but I do think that if the federal district commission is going to expropriate property all around Ottawa, I am not blaming them for that, because someone might make money improperly if he knew the exact details-it should tell the owners of that property that 'they will not be moved unless and until the services of transportation, sewage, water and the like have been provided in their area.
There is another matter in connection with expropriation which I should like to mention.
I have had considerable difficulty in explaining to people how hard it is to settle the amounts

they are to receive for their houses. I must confess I am not at all pleased with the methods being followed by the federal district commission in settling the amounts to be paid to residential owners around this city. I must say it is done in an odd fashion. Those who are hired by the federal district commission to set the prices simply bring these people to their offices and say, ""Well, you will get so much; if you do not like it you can go to the courts-and it will take five years."" That is not the way to deal with these matters. Surely when people are taken from their homes in order to enlarge a capital city they should be given every benefit and the prices should be such as to compensate them for the building of new houses, for the trouble of being displaced.

I wish to bring this matter to the attention of the Prime Minister. I believe if we are to displace people from the capital city, they should be treated as fairly and as well as possible. I may have some further remarks to make when we are considering the estimates.

I should like to add that in addition to the physical development of the capital city we should think of its cultural and spiritual values. I should like the capital city of Canada to be an example of national unity and of Canadian citizenship. Surely this is the place where one should not find those narrow ideas, those narrow differences between factions. Because people who will come here in the future, after so much money has been spent on this beautiful city, and after so much has been spent in the development of the capital area, whether they come from elsewhere in Canada or from other parts of the world, will expect to find at least within this area a true picture of healthy Canadian citizenship.

,Liberal,,Jean-Thomas Richard,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a990e2af-c044-40da-880c-510347167930&Language=E&Section=ALL

BLACKMORE (Lethbridge):,,QUESTIONS,NATIONAL CAPITAL,DEVELOPMENT UNDER APPROVED PLAN-PROVISION FOR ANNUAL APPROPRIATIONS,Mr. Speaker, I hope in the few remarks I shall make I shall be able to remain strictly nonpartisan, and that I shall speak on a plane befitting the subject matter of the resolution -the building of a capital for a great nation of the future.

In the first place I believe an unfair reflection has been cast upon the city of Ottawa. True, there are defects in Ottawa as a city. People have not got things quite the way they would like to have them; on that we can agree. None of us has. But, all things being considered, I suggest the people of Ottawa have done admirably' well. When one recalls that Ottawa began as Bytown only eighty years ago, and when by' looking at some of the relics of those day's he acquires some idea of
Development of National Capital
wlbat Bytown must have been like, he must conclude that the eity of Ottawa is worthy of the highest praise.

I should like to congratulate the people of this city upon their superb good senise in planting and retaining beautiful trees throughout the city, so that one who walks through the city may wailk through one magnificent park, as it were. The city has not yielded to some of the silly fade which have nowadays become the vogue in some parts, one of which has been to out down trees. On the contrary the people of this city have kept its trees, wherever they could keep them-trees which anyone must admire, even if in some instances the houses are second or third rate. In making these observations I have been no more than fair to the city of Ottawa.

The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is to be congratulated upon his part- in Ottawa's development, and I Should like also to congratulate him upon the speech he made today. It was on a high plane, and, I thought, in all respects admirable. I enjoyed listening to it; I thought it was as a speech of that kind should have been. Indeed I felt several times that if the speech is read by our descendants a hundred, years from today they will view with pleasure and satisfaction his treatment of the matter in this year 1948.

Canada is not a populous country. When we undertake to appraise what has been achieved in this capital city we must remember that Canada has plenty of drawbacks. She has had them, nationally, ever since she started to keep house. She has not really teamed yet how to manage her own house. There is still a tremendous amount of disagreement as to how it Should be done. No wonder she does not yet know exactly how to do it. But we are learning, and we shall learn, if it please the Lord, until some of these days we shall run this glorious country the way we want to see it run, and believe it should be run.

Perhaps we can be expected to do a little more, and do it faster, than we have done it up to .the present time. Let us not forget, however, that since the turn of the century we have been through two terrible wars. During fifty years of the time this has been the capital city we have experienced wars, depressions, crop failures, and the like. In estimating what has been achieved, these facts must not be forgotten.

It. is well to plan our national capital with an eye to the year 2048, as the Prime Minister suggested. It is well to remember, as he stated, that, Canada is to continue free and independent as a member of the British empire. There are some who are looking forward eagerly and almost with watering mouths to a
time when we shall be gobbled up by the United States. The Prime Minister expressed no such anxiety, no such pessimism.

This nation shall continue great and free. We can be proud and thankful to live in Canada. Canada will become populous, powerful, self-sufficient, wealthy, generous, respected. beloved by all nations, and a great and good neighbour. All these characteristics she has shown during the last fifty years. God blessed us with the natural resources to enable us to do these things, and has placed us in a combination of nations, the British commonwealth and empire, which if we know how to use our opportunities will enable us to accomplish great things, using the resources that God gave us as we desire to use them.

I think all of this was hinted, and appropriately so, in the speech of the Prime Minister. Although he did not indicate it specifically, I think I glimpsed the vision that the British commonwealth is not something that is finished. When he spoke of the little land of England as being the spiritual mother of those people called British, for hundreds, if not thousands of years-he did not mention the years, but I do-I think he was simply expressing justifiable faith in the future of those people, in the future of the combination of people known as the British commonwealth, which has continued as a force for general good and which merits therefore the blessings of Almighty God to the extent that it shall prevail over its enemies and become the blessing to all. men in future centuries that it has been during the last two centuries.
All this should be borne in mind when we plan our capital city, the capital which perhaps is to be the national centre of the foremost member of that glorious galaxy of nations, the British empire.

All that is necessaiy is intelligence and good will in co-operating with men of good will in other parts of the empire. All we need, coupled with the resources, rich and varied, of this and other British countries, is the courage to stand up for the things we believe in, and to insist that other peoples shall not ""shoulder us around"". Then we shall achieve superb and magnificent realities.

It is well that we bear all these things in mind when we plan for the city of Ottawa. I do not advocate too rapid expenditure. It is wise to look far ahead and to spend only as we feel we can afford to spend. We should spend wisely, building soundly and well, so that people looking back on our works two hundred years from now may be glad that we at this particular time in history were here as members of parliament in Ottawa.

KNIGHT (Saskatoon City):,,QUESTIONS,NATIONAL CAPITAL,DEVELOPMENT UNDER APPROVED PLAN-PROVISION FOR ANNUAL APPROPRIATIONS,Mr. Speaker, I have to follow the eloquence of the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more), and I am quite diffident about mentioning the subject that I want to bring up at this time, because it throws a discordant touch of colour into the fine picture which has been painted for us by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King).

We notice that in the beautification of cities an effort is generally made to let nature have some hand in the business. We attempt to decentralize our cities and the works of man. We first crowd into places and they are developed on the basis of real estate sold at so much per square foot. Later on we sometimes repent our labours, or perhaps our sins, and proceed to change the whole business and let nature come in with some of that healing which she is ever ready to operate to overcome the mistakes of man.

The house may be wondering what I am leading up to. I am referring to certain things that have been done to make this fine city ugly in appearance. Perhaps I shall shock members of this house, particularly those representing Ottawa, when I say that when I close my eyes and think of this city I can see only the great signs that appear here and there in the area contiguous to the city, particularly among the fields and woods where they are so incongruous.

Then when I go out Bank street, I see many of these little juke-box joints. It seems to me that in these days of building material shortages they do not need building materials to put up these places, because they are literally covered with advertisements for various kinds of soft drinks. If they' would advertise with quiet colours, or try to follow some natural scheme, perhaps I would not find such great fault; but for some reason commercialism believes in sensationalism, in the use of glaring and horrible colours. I never could understand why a farmer living among the beauties of nature with a fine orchard at his back door and stream at the front would allow someone to cover his barn with signs advertising chewing tobacco or laxatives. Either article may be estimable and necessary for the adult and baby population of the country, but personally I cannot understand why advertising of it in this way is encouraged.

May I say a word to these gentlemen who so advertise their wares? I drive a car but I avoid buying gasoline which is advertised by this particular method. One of the several reasons why I purchase nothing from a certain great commercial firm in Toronto, not unconnected with the business of mail order, is
that they persist in making the country ugly, particularly the vicinity of Toronto, with great signs advertising their wares.

Perhaps we can do nothing about this thing in the city, but I think any commission or other body having the responsibility for the general beautification of Ottawa should start a campaign to get rid of these things in its vicinity. Having got rid of them they should proceed to beautify according to their plan. The use of glaring and screaming colours by crude and vulgar commercialism should be done away with.

Tourists come here and they judge us largely by what they see. That is fair enough. There is every justification for so doing. But personally I do not care to be judged by the type of thing that one sees in our valleys and along our wooded areas. Incidentally many people from outside our country come here to get away from that sort of thing-the glaring signs in their own cities and juke-box joints which unfortunately are also becoming a part of our national life. My plea would be for a return to plain and decent things, the things of nature which can be used to beautify our cities.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Robert Ross (Roy) Knight,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=f2bbf383-7eb4-4502-a636-9fe5ed8129ea&Language=E&Section=ALL
1542032,ca.proc.d.1948-06-28.2.5.1.49,1948-06-28,a519c7ba-e092-4c85-95fb-2519b2cbfc06,ca.m.8326,Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,QUESTIONS,NATIONAL CAPITAL,DEVELOPMENT UNDER APPROVED PLAN-PROVISION FOR ANNUAL APPROPRIATIONS,Mr. Speaker, the resolution before the house attempts to set out the attitude that this and later parliaments should take with respect to future support of the national capital. This is a resolution which I think should be approached in a non-partisan way. I should hate to think that it would ever be made a partisan issue, because I think every member of this house and every political party wants to do what it is proper the Canadian nation should do for its capital-that much, neither more nor less.

This resolution having to do with the development of the capital of Canada, and having been put in this form in our records, I think we should examine in detail what its passage means and how it will be interpreted later on by the Canadian people and by the city of Ottawa.

I want to commend the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for his interest in this project; but when I say that I want also to say that I would not like to think that any man in Canada has a monopoly of interest in the development of this capital. I think every member desires parliament to do what is appropriate for the development of Ottawa as the national capital.
The resolution consists of a preamble of four clauses, and four clauses in the main
Development oj National Capital
body of the resolution. The first clause of the preamble recites:
That whereas the requirements of a national capital involve, from time to time, developments of a character beyond the municipal improvements ordinarily required in other cities . . .
I think that proposition is obviously one which parliament can accept and approve.
The second clause of the preamble reads:
And whereas the development of a national capital is at least in part a national responsibility . . .
That, too, I think is obvious to every member of the house and to every Canadian.
The third clause reads:
And whereas the capital of Canada is designated by the British North America Act to be Ottawa . . .
Even the most partisan among us can find no objection to that simple statement of fact.
The last clause of the preamble reads:
And whereas the carrying out of planned improvements requires a clear expression of intention to proceed with necessary developments in a manner which will ensure continuity . . .

That clause I think requires a little more critical examination, so that we may understand what it means and so that the Canadian people will understand what we are doing if and when we pass this resolution. It calls for a clear expression of intention to proceed with necessary developments in a manner which will ensure continuity. I suggest that the only intention which this house can express is the intention of the present house. We may express the hope that those who may follow us in this parliament five, ten, fifteen, twenty or a hundred years from now will have the same view; and I am optimistic enough to believe they will have. But in any event nothing we can say in this house today can commit parliament five or ten or twenty or fifty years from now to doing something it does not want to do.

We can only have faith that those who will succeed us in this parliament will approach this problem just as sensibly as we do. Speaking for myself and those associated with me, we are willing now to express our intention to do what is proper in connection with the development of the national capital. From time to time there will be differences of opinion as to just what should be done, and how much should be done, and how much should be spent. But nothing we may say here now will prevent questions of that kind from arising in the future.
The preamble ends with these words:
-to proceed with necessary developments in a manner which will ensure continuity.

We may hope that the passage of this resolution will ensure some continuity, and I fully expect it will, but there may be differences of opinion as to just what the words ""will ensure continuity"" mean. If we start out on a reasonable plan now, I am sure that it will be accepted in principle by any parliament which may follow us; but with respect to details, or with respect to the generosity of future parliaments as regards certain aspects of any plan we might approve now, we cannot speak for them.
I come now to the main body of the resolution, the first clause of which reads:
That it is desirable that all developments of the capital should be in accordance with an approved plan . . .

Some question was raised about that, and the Prime Minister indicated that he would give further information when his estimates are under consideration. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that before this resolution is passed we ought to give a little more consideration to just what those words mean. I ask myself: Where is this approved plan, and what is it? We here now may say that we think such-and-such a plan is a good one, and that we approve the appropriation of a certain amount of money for the purpose of carrying it out; but I suggest that we cannot tie ourselves now to some ""approved plan"", the details of which we do not know. We can approve the principle, and say that the general attitude of parliament ought to be such-and-such towards this project, but I do not think we should be asked to tie ourselves now to some approved plan the details of which we have not seen, and which in any case in the very nature of things must change from time to time.

For example, I pass by Confederation square every morning. At some time in the past somebody thought that, was a good plan for Ottawa. I wonder whether everybody thinks so today. I wonder whether that is the final plan for that section of the city of Ottawa. It must be clear that we cannot make any plan now which will be good for all time to come, in a nation which in twenty-five or .fifty or a hundred years we hope will be vastly greater than Canada is today, and with a capital which will grow as the nation grows.
The second clause in the main body of the resolution reads:

That a special account in the consolidated revenue fund, to be known as the national capital fund, should be created, to which appropriation may he made annually by parliament over a period of .years.

That is simply a matter of bookkeeping which we need not take time to debate. It is a clause we can all accept.
The next clause reads:
That it is desirable that the work necessary to this end be under the supervision of the federal district commission, distinct from its ordinary operations ...

Some body must be given charge of the administration of this project, and I imagine that the federal district commission is as well fitted for the purpose as any other, if not better. I see no need for any other special body being created for this purpose.
The fourth and last clause of the resolution reads:
That the expenditure of moneys for these purposes should be conditional on the effective co-operation of the city of Ottawa and other municipalities within the national capital district.

The intent of that clause is I think reasonable and desirable, but I question whether it is essential. Are we to be tied up in the development of the national capital because there might be some disputes between the municipalities affected? Surely not. Surely means could be found through which these institutions, these municipalities-which are all interested, as we are, in the wisest plans to follow-could be brought together without tying our hands here as to what we shall do in case there may be dissension between certain of them.

A question has arisen in this debate as to the relative importance of expenditures on a national capital-as to whether we should commit ourselves now to support plans for a national capital, while certain other projects, such as highways, housing, national security measures, and so on, require additional support. Questions such as these are questions which every parliament must face. I would be disappointed if, when this resolution passes, either in its exact form or in some modified form, the Canadian people interpret it to mean that the parliament of Canada is undertaking to enter upon an extravagant plan for the development of this city. I would be disappointed if they take it to mean that we are to take off the city of Ottawa its proper share of the development of the city. I would be disappointed if they take it to mean that we are going to do something here, and leave something else that is more important uncompleted or only partly done.
If this resolution passes I will not put that interpretation on it. If this resolution passes what it will mean is that I, as one member of the parliament of Canada, am saying that

in the development of a national capital we should have some idea where we are going. We should lay plans that will prevent waste in the future. We should try to look ahead and lay plans that those who follow us will be proud of; and that we should help-no more and no less than to the extent that in a national capital the nation itself should contribute; that much, and no more.

I would not like to think that anybody in the city of Ottawa wants to draw from the parliament of Canada more than should be given to the city. On the other hand, I would hate to think that the parliament of Canada wants to lean on the people of the municipality in which the national capital happens to be. We must have some faith in one another, and some faith in the future. If I were to express the wishes of the Canadian people as I learn them from one end of Canada to the other, it is that we expect the parliament of Canada to bear its full share of the development of the national capital. The people -want to see here a capital of which they will be proud. But they do not wont to see us enter upon wildly extravagant plans while there are many other necessary things to do in every part of the countiy.

I would not support this resolution if extravagant expenditure around this city is what the resolution is to be interpreted as meaning; and the Canadian people would not support it. If we proceed with a cautious plan, one that is not extravagant, one that is carefully thought out, it will appeal to the Canadian people, and they will want to support it. But to the extent that we go beyond that, there will be resistance to appropriations from year to year. I should not like to think that any more is read into this resolution than that the parliament of Canada will be fair to the constituency in which the capital finds itself, and will be fair to its own future in having as its capital a capital of which the Canadian people would be proud.

I have just one practical suggestion to make. The resolution refers to an approved plan. I doubt whether hon. members are familiar with the details of even the plans that are now said to be in existence. I would point out that we are putting on the permanent record a resolution which has to do with the development of Canada's capital now and for the long future, and it is only an hour and a half since it was introduced. I suggest that the passage of this resolution would mean more and would be accepted more generally- not that anybody is going -to oppose its passage-if, when the Prime Minister's
Development of National Capital

estimates come up, we could have a full discussion of the details with respect to the present plans that have been spoken of as the master plan. 'Let us hope that whatever plan there is, it is in fact a master plan, and that everything that we can see from this vantage point is considered. But I suggest-that the resolution would mean much more to Canada if its final passage were left until after the discussion takes place on the details when the Prime Minister's estimates are up for discussion.

,Progressive Conservative,,John Bracken,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a519c7ba-e092-4c85-95fb-2519b2cbfc06&Language=E&Section=ALL
1542033,ca.proc.d.1948-06-28.2.5.1.50,1948-06-28,20afcc72-88d0-433e-8b61-a7bcd98b2ec9,ca.m.3746,Mr. G. J. McILRAITH (Ottawa West):,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,QUESTIONS,NATIONAL CAPITAL,DEVELOPMENT UNDER APPROVED PLAN-PROVISION FOR ANNUAL APPROPRIATIONS,As the member of the Canadian House of Commons for the electoral district in which the parliament buildings are situated, I should like at the very outset to say to hon. members how pleased I am that this resolution is now being dealt with. To me it represents a most important further milestone along the way of developing our national capital, a subject in which I have taken deep interest, not only before I was a member of the House of Commons, but also in the eight years since I was first elected as a member of this house.

I should like to think that the development of the national capital is something of great interest to all Canadian citizens. I should also like to think that as it is developed it will be developed in such a way as to epitomize the legitimate expression of the ambitions of all Canadian citizens.

At the outset perhaps I should say a word about the form of the resolution. I am particularly pleased to notice that it is presented for the consideration of parliament in the form of a resolution rather than as a rigid bill, with a grant of money to be spent over a certain number of years. It seems to me that the present method provides for that important element of control by parliament over the expenditures from year to year. By this method now adopted, parliament can examine into the particular circumstances as they exist from year to year. Parliament can examine the expenditures with relation to other items of public expenditures that may be made or that may be of lesser or more importance as circumstances exist at the time. Perhaps this is an effective answer to the questions raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) when he spoke of certain other matters that require consideration and expenditure of public funds. The present method leaves control in parliament and also provides the opportunity for annual discussion and examination.
One point was made by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Boucher) with which I think I ought to deal. With his remarks

I was, in the main, quite in accord, but he referred to the development of certain parts by the provinces or for the provinces. I have no quarrel with that idea, except to say that it is the national capital that we are seeking to develop. It is fortunate that it is located on the edge of a great river forming the interprovincial boundary between two large and important provinces, certainly two of the most populous, which have attained a high degree of development. It is the conception of the capital as representing all the people of Canada, the nation's capital, that I would like to see emphasized, rather than something representing each province separately.

In other words, while I am strongly for provincial rights in their own field, I do not think this is the place to bring them forward and to emphasize divisions with respect to them. After all, our great political problem in Canada is the problem of geography. Surely, in the development of the plan for our national capital, we should refrain from over-emphasizing the difficulties of the problem of geography.

One -other thing is this. I would be sorry to see a certain area -allocated to each province, for the reason that there might develop a situation wherein one province, because of financial difficulties-and provinces occasionally do have financial difficulties-owing to its lack of -ability to spend money as generously as other provinces, would have a poorer development. I do not think we should permit that to happen. If we did permit that sort of thing it would tend to emphasize differences between provinces, and it would give rise to a feeling the opposite of pride on the part of this or that province in . what it had been able to accomplish. I do not think any of -us would want -that to happen.

The northern half of this continent is now a great nation, and our development should be such as to bring the position of that nation to the forefront in the world today. We should not do anything that would tend to divide the nation or make it appear as if it were a collection of little Balkam-like states. So far as the other parts of the remarks made by the hon. member for Carleton are concerned, I am in complete accord.

I was disappointed in the attitude taken by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, the leader of the C.C.F. party. I must say frankly I had hoped that over the years we had developed to the point where hon. members in all parts of the house were interested in the national capital as such, and I can only say to the hon. member-I regret he is not ini his seat at the moment-that I was disappointed when he sought to treat this as a small matter of partisan advantage one way or the other.

1542036,ca.proc.d.1948-06-28.2.5.1.53,1948-06-28,62287d4a-32a2-4734-a1b3-18cce52da443,ca.m.5390,Mr. GILLIS:,,QUESTIONS,NATIONAL CAPITAL,DEVELOPMENT UNDER APPROVED PLAN-PROVISION FOR ANNUAL APPROPRIATIONS,He was talking about the trans-Canada highway.
AL-. McILRAITH:
column2: I was here, listening

column1: intently to the debate, and I heard it all. I was disappointed that the leader of the hon. gentleman's party should have seen fit to go into such side issues as the matter of highway construction. That is another matter altogether, and I certainly do not wish to discuss it now. Surely, in the development of the nation's capital, we can take a position that will preclude this constant attempt to go into by-paths and to raise questions of partisan advantage, claiming that this or that party has been more interested in certain social welfare matters, such as the development of housing in Ottawa. That is not good enough. It is not relevant to this question, so far as the development of housing is concerned, I do not take second place to the hon. gentleman or any of his party in my interest in it. I do not see why that question cannot be discussed in its proper place. I for one am frank to admit that things in the 'city of Ottawa are not all as they should be. Of course they are not. There are a great many things which I should like to see done to improve conditions for our people; but we can deal with these things each in its proper place, instead of seeking to prejudice a great cause like this in the minds of one segment or another of the population for the purpose of gaining party advantage at the moment. Surely the conception can be a little broader than that, and I hope it will be.

As to the resolution itself, it is also pleasing to me to note that the Prime Minister of Canada has brought it forward. Over the years I have come to know and to appreciate the great part which the Prime Minister has played in advancing this country, as a nation, to the high position which it now holds among the nations. I recognize the great conception he has had for the development of the national capital, and it is for that
reason I now express gratitude that circumstances are such that the present Prime Minister has introduced this resolution.

There are two more points I wish to discuss. Reference has been made from time to time to certain constituencies, or to certain municipal corporations. The whole scheme of the development of the capital involves a great many municipal corporations. The constant reference seems to be to Ottawa-Ottawa- Ottawa. I do not know whether it is less or more than half, but a relatively large part of the development is outside Ottawa altogether. I do not know' whether more than half of it is outside Ottawa in terms of dollars, but certainly much more than half of it is outside the city in terms of area and of developmental work to be done. It is therefore not simply a matter of one municipality.

Different municipalities have their problems as related to this one. They are acute problems, and it is a mistake to minimize them. But they have come forward writh a degree of co-operation that promises well for the future development of the scheme. The question whether this municipality or that should do this thing or that- is not something that can be dealt with here on a general resolution. Rather it is a question of deciding with the working staff such details as supplies, services and so on. In that connection, however, I should like to point out one thing. When this scheme was first being talked about, some of the municipalities seemed to feel that their own rights in local municipal matters were being interfered with. That fear has pretty well disappeared since it has come to be realized that it is not a matter of taking away any municipal rights at all. Rather it is a matter of leaving the municipalities all their rights in local matters, but trying to co-ordinate such matters to fit into the great national scheme, so that they will be part of a general pattern, as opposed to individual local questions not related one to the other.

It is perhaps well to realize, Mr. Speaker, that the status Canada has achieved as a nation in the world today has been won by the sacrifices of her soldiers in two world wrars. I hope the future development of this capital will be such as to please, in particular, those of our soldiers who have returned, and to express the feelings and ambitions, with respect to their country, of those who served their nation in the armed forces in two world wars.
