DIEFENBAKER (Lake Centre):,,QUESTIONS,MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE,,"Mr. Speaker, on Saturday evening at the time of the adjournment I had begun to refer to the various recommendations, and to the circumstances that it was peculiar that the recommendations contained in the report were first brought to the attention of the government members of the committee-some of them, rather-almost one week before they were brought to the attention of the Progressive Conservative members of that committee. I

referred among other things to the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in his opposition to the committee's making recommendations; to this he took some objection. I referred to the pages in Hansard, and I shall now read what the Prime Minister said in that regard. On page 749 of Hansard we find this:
Mr. Lockhart: What about recommendations?
Mr. Mackenzie King:
column2: My hon. friend asks

column1: about recommendations. I am glad he mentioned that, because that was the next criticism I was going to refer to. May I say that hon. gentlemen opposite have taken exception to the resolution not specifying that the committee should bring in recommendations. May I say that at this stage the obligation was left out deliberately by the government, and for this reason. If it had been added that the committee were to make recommendations we would now be hearing from hon. gentlemen opposite, and they would have been speaking correctly, that the minute you give to a committee of this kind the business of making recommendations, that minute you are certain to start all kinds of political controversy.
I pause here to ask: what difference did it make whether that power was granted at the time the Prime Minister spoke, of later?

You start issues of policy making. You would start pros and cons between members of the committee as to whether this recommendation should be made or that, and the time of the committee instead of being used for the purpose of getting at the facts would be used for the purpose of trying to bring forward one particular policy or another. I say this, that if the committee, after they have been at work for some time and have the facts before them, feel that they would like to have their powers enlarged and be given the opportunity to bring in recommendations, I for one shall be very happy to further a purpose of the kind.

The recommendations were made, regardless of whether power was granted or not. I again ask the Prime Minister when he speaks, as the press report says he will: why did those recommendations have their origin outside the committee?

I come now to what I was dealing with the other evening. What is the government going to do about these recommendations? It should not wait until next year or next session, but should act in the present session; because the prices situation is accelerating month by month-accelerating at a rate that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) indicated last November would not be arrived at at any time. I ask the Prime Minister this-for, after all, it is the government which must take the responsibility-why is it that some action has not been taken with respect to prices? Is it because the government of Canada is afraid of what the United States might say about prices in this country? I shall not
Report oj Prices Committee

quote the exact words in another debate, because to do so is not in accordance with the rules; I refer to what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) said on May 26, 1948, as reported at pages 4396 and 4397 of Hansard, wherein he indicated that if Canada were to act, it might be taken in the United States as action that would not contribute to international good relationships.

I cannot understand why Canada should allow the determination of what our price levels should be, or what the action taken by the government should be, to be controlled by what another nation might wish or desire. But it does indicate this, that again we have the same old story of the top bureaucracy of this country-I might call it the gilt top bureaucracy-over and over again following a policy made in Washington, and making it applicable to Canada.
Here is what the Minister of Finance said, speaking in New York in January last, when he was questioned as to what the government was going to do about prices:
It is possible that there might be selective reimposition of price control, but that will depend on what parliament decides and what may happen down here.

Surely parliament should determine in Canada what the needs of Canadians should be, and what should be done in regard to this matter, instead of abdicating in favour of another country the right to determine for Canada what is good for Canadians.

Sometimes I wonder what the government's policy is. On November 17 last the Prime Minister spoke in a radio broadcast, and told of the new world that had arrived. You could just see the trade barriers falling down. You could see 400,000 Canadian cattle marching across the line into the United States. But hardly had he concluded his broadcast when the Minister of Finance went on the air and said, in effect, ""Not yet; not yet; not yet!"" The Prime Minister with one policy; one of his ministers with another.
In February last the Minister of Finance, apparently believing the difficulties were solved, speaking in the city of Brantford said this:
It is too early yet to start throwing our hats in the air, but it iooks as if the downward price trend this week in the United States might mark the turning point.
Again, Canada depending for a solution of her policies upon what is occurring in the United States. The report continues:
He said the Canadian price trend would follow that of the United States in any longterm movement because the economies of the two countries were so closely linked.

Over and over again the government expressed the hope for, but did not act to achieve, some measure of increase in production in this country to the end that a reasonable price level would thereby be attained.

What is the government's policy on this subject? If I quoted someone other than a supporter of the government, it might be argued that I was giving prejudiced evidence. I shall refer to a speech made the other day by one who is often spoken of as another heir apparent, Mr. Stuart Carson, Premier of Manitoba. What he said represents the criticism of the leader of the opposition and of this party regarding the prices of agricultural products. He attacked the federal government and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) for treating the provincial governments like a "" lot of robots."" Premier Drew has said that on occasions; Premier Duplessis on occasions; and now the Premier of Manitoba, a supporter of this government, says that the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the federal government have endeavoured to treat the provincial governments like a lot of robots.

I quote from a summary of a report of Mr. Garson's speech and bring it to the attention of the Prime Minister. Mr. Garson emphasized that the farmers could no longer be asked to continue as the only large economic unit whose prices are under government control. He declared that the wheat board as now constituted was another instrument of the government which was acting contrary to the farmer's interest in their policy of closing off the markets of the United States to Canadian farmers and offering farm products to Great Britain at low prices and then requiring the farmer to bear the burden of those lower prices.

The Premier of Manitoba took the same view that this party takes, that there can be no objection to assistance being given to Great Britain, provided that it is given by the people as a whole and not placed as a responsibility upon the farmers of this country.

I should like now to refer to a few of these recommendations. There is a vote of 850,000 in the supplementary estimates to cover the cost of a royal commission on prices. A committee of parliament has sat for four months and has made recommendations that somebody else prepared for them. Why the necessity, why the need for a royal commission, except that the government again wants to postpone action on this matter? These delaying tactics can have but one result; they place parliament in contempt of the people of this country.
Report oj Prices Committee

Let us act; let us stay here until something is done. The responsibility rests primarily upon the Prime Minister and the government. I say it rests upon the Prime Minister, because in today's issue of the Financial Post there is an article by Kenneth Wilson in which it is stated that nothing is being done, that the government is not showing any leadership because of the divergent viewpoints among those who would be heirs apparent. The Prime Minister, having only two or three months, or whatever the length of time may be, to lead the government, is not giving to those who support him in this house the leadership in this matter that he is capable of. Recommendation No. 3 reads:

That the government amend the regulations of the appropriate legislation, if that be found necessary, so that immediate specific action can be taken wherever the evidence discloses flagrant cases of profiteering at the consumer's expense.

Why has not the government acted up to now? It has the wartime prices and trade board. I am not going to refer in detail to the regulations of that board, except to say that sections 3 and 8 give the board absolute power. All that has been done about this challenge of profiteering since the committee was set up is to be found in recommendation No. 3, where it says:
The work of investigation and fact-finding
I would almost say fault-finding.
-already undertaken by the committee has resulted in twelve prosecutions of those profiteering in butter, with three convictions already registered.
Then it goes on:
In addition, proceedings have been instituted in five cases of profiteering in the fruit and vegetable industry.

Does that look like a serious endeavour to prosecute exploitation? Does that look as if the government or this board wants to act? The report indicates that there is evidence of profiteering in some cases, but it does not name the wrongdoers. I remember that when the Prime Minister spoke in February he said that if there was one thing that would prevent a rise in the cost of living-I am merely generalizing-it was fear of exposure of profiteering interests. Where is there fear of exposure in saying that there were some eases, somewhere, some place, and then leaving it to each of us to look through 3,000 pages of evidence in order to ascertain where they were.
The next recommendation reads:
That the government consider the removal of import restrictions now in effect on certain fruits and vegetables . . .

I ask the Prime Minister: Did the United States department of state make representations to the government of Canada that the embargo on fruits and vegetables should be removed? That is what the United States press says the government of the United States did recently.
Another recommendation reads:
The government should give consideration to the desirability and practicability of restricting price rises by special taxation of unreasonable profits.

Is that going to frighten anybody unless it is acted upon? If that is the solution, does the government, intend to introduce measures at this session, or does it intend to wait six or eight months longer, while prices pyramid, before taking any action? It must be remembered that the government cannot say that it has not a solution, because one of the policies laid down at the Liberal convention of 1919 was this: Give us a chance and we will show you how to control high prices. Now prices are higher than they ever were during or after the first world war, at a time when there were no such controls as existed during the last war.
There cannot be any dispute about the recommendation in connection with business accounting, but it is a strange thing that it took three long years to find' that out. The next recommendation reads:

Was that recommendation just so much verbiage, to lead the people to -believe that something more was to be done? Are we to wait six months before anything is done? Are you going to act upon it in this parliament, or are you going to act again by order in council?
Then after recommending what should be done, the committee finds another loophole, for section II of the report says:
The committee realizes that in the long run the federal government may be faced with constitutional difficulties in regard to its operations in the field of prices.
You see, Mr. Speaker, how it goes. They take a line, and then deviate a little from it.
Report oj Prices Committee

They say what should be done immediately. They say that consideration should be given, but add, in effect: Remember that if we do not act, in the long run. it will be because we cannot act on account of constitutional difficulties. It is interesting to note that the government are starting to abandon the doctrine of emergency, on which they placed so much reliance. Will the Prime Minister say whether the provinces are being consulted? Will he say whether, if prices can be controlled, it requires the assistance of the provinces? If so, why does not the government bring in a measure such as it did on barley and oats, which required correlative legislation by the provinces to make the federal legislation effective? What has the government done about communicating with the provinces? While Manitoba was not very anxious to co-operate on oats and barley because the premier of the province saw through the sham, I am sure that every province would join and give assistance in solving the problem of the high price level which bears down on all our people.
Here is the next recommendation:

That the government, in considering the removal of existing embargoes on the exportation of food products from Canada, give careful study to the supply situation here, and the proper balance to be maintained between the interests of both producers and consumers.

I do not know whether this has anything to do with the 400.000 head of cattle for which entry is promised under the Geneva agreements, or whether it has reference to some qualified promises which have been made lately that the embargo on cattle is to be lifted. While some government supporters say the embargo is to be lifted, the committee says to the government: Watch out; give it further consideration. That is just another example, sir, of that diversity in a disunited cabinet of which we have seen so much evidence during the last three or four months.
The next recommendation is this:

That the government instruct the dominion bureau of statistics to publish periodically an analysis showing the way in which the consumer's dollar is divided among the various elements which enter into the price of basic commodities.

Another good recommendation. Why has it not been done? If it is done, it will be the best answer to my hon. friends to the left who spend their time preaching about how much of the dollar actually consists of profits to those who place their capital in industry.

The record in the United States clearly indicated in a recent survey that the statements made by my hon. friends of the C.C.F. have no justification there, and I say, according to the evidence placed before the committee, that, excepting those nameless corporations who stand condemned in the report, industry as a whole in this country today is receiving but a fair share of the total consumer dollar. What is our recommendation? First, remove the excise tax. One of the reasons why the standard of living of the people in the lower income brackets is going down is that they are caught in a squeeze between taxation, which is taking 23 cents out of every dollar of the total income in the country, and rising prices, from which no relief to speak of was given this year. Second, the time has come for action, before the present session is concluded, to give relief in the matter of income taxes so that our people may be able to spend the largest possible portion of their income rather than have the government spend it for them.

The report seems to me to be an innocuous thing, a thing almost of pure expediency, which was designed by the government and perhaps foisted upon the committee to bolster the failing fortunes of a party that has become bankrupt of ideas, and certainly bankrupt in the courage necessary to meet a situation that has become nothing short of a crisis in this country. As a result of that lack of constructive ideas and of courage the people are drifting into a feeling of frustration, in which condition they fall prey to socialists and communists, with all their cunning and all their fanatical energy. The country is seriously endangered thereby. The signs are there, and I challenge the government to warn the people and to take heed themselves before it is too late.

Now a word about taxes and how they affect the whole price situation. I am told that on a number of occasions in the committee, though I was not a member of it, companies coming before the committee to give evidence were asked to make submissions on the taxes they were required to pay to the various governments. I have one such statement supplied by a Canadian company to which I shall refer later.

In the main, one of the greatest reasons for the high cost of living is and has been taxation. That is a matter about which the government can do something. It is a matter about which the government has been warned time and time again, but regarding which it has done nothing. High onerous taxation goes on, and as a result of that high onerous taxation, if anyone will take the trouble to investigate the selling price of a single one of the hundreds of articles in common daily use, he will find that the taxes imposed by the various governments in Canada make up from 80 to 90 per cent of the total price paid by consumers. That seems a very high percentage, but it has been proved to be true on a number of occasions.
Report oj Prices Committee

It is true with regard, let us say, to gasoline and oils that are used by farmers and industrialists and people generally in the course of production. I am not referring entirely to gasoline and oil used by pleasure travellers. It has been shown by expert investigators that fully 80 per cent of the total consumer price of a gallon of gasoline goes to the various governments in taxes. It can 'be shown that up to 95 per cent of the total consumer price of a good many articles that Canadians use from day to day, which enter into their overall cost of living, is taken in taxes by the various governments. That makes it obvious that if you are going to do anything worthwhile about the cost of living, the place to start is in the direction of taxation.

Let me refer for a moment to a return which was made to the prices committee on June 21 in relation to this very question of taxation. Here is a letter from Canadian Celanese Company Limited, signed by A. G. Allen, treasurer:
Mr. Fabio Monet, K.C.,
Counsel to the Special Committee on Prices, House of Commons, Ottawa Dear Sir,
In reply to the request made hy Mr. Kuhl, we are pleased to list below the details of taxes charged against income for the year 1947, totalling $2,794,460.95.
And here is the breakdown:
Dominion of Canada income and
excess profits taxes.. $2,167,000.90
Dominion sales and excise taxes
Provincial taxes on income and
_ capital
Provincial tax on purchases ....
Municipal taxes
Miscellaneous

Of course that represents only taxes paid directly by the company to these various collecting agencies. It does not take into consideration at all the percentage of payments eventually appearing as taxes which the company makes directly to railways and other transportation companies and those giving service in the production and distribution to the consumer of the goods the company produces; a percentage of tax content which often runs to fifty and sixty per cent of the total consumer price of the goods. Every railway carrying this company's goods pays a large amount of taxes to these three taxing authorities, municipal, provincial and dominion, and such taxes are not included at all in this statement. The letter goes on:

As the total sales for 1947 were $17,531,957, we calculate that if we had paid no taxes in this year a reduction in the sales price of our products of 15-9 per cent would have yielded the same net profit which we obtained in 1947.

That is a pertinent statement, and is the best evidence I could possibly give of the pyramiding effect of taxation such as we have in this country. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the cost of living in Canada could be reduced fully twenty per cent within a period of months through a wise and carefully planned reduction in taxation. That fact ought to be driven home with all the force we can muster; and the people should unite in their demand for an immediate beginning in tax reduction.

In the press I have noticed that considerable emphasis has been placed on the representations made by Ontario Liberals to the Prime Minister to drop the 25 per cent excise tax. More than two months ago the Social Credit League of Ontario sent a letter to every member of this parliament demanding the removal of that excise tax, and further asking for an immediate start in the reduction of taxation of all kinds which tends to push up prices and causes the cost of living to get out of control. Again I point out that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) moved an amendment to the speech from the throne in which he advocated substantial tax reduction as a means of bringing down living costs. Moreover, on May 21 of this year I presented to the house a social credit budget in contrast to the one brought down by the Minister of Finance. In it I emphasized proposals which would lead to tax reduction as a means of price reduction. In that speech, and in those given in support of my budget, proposals by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more) and the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), we showed in detail how the reductions could be made without in any way affecting the services given the people of Canada. We did not suggest particularly at that time the introduction of anything that could not be introduced in this country with safety; and we are not now suggesting that the cure-all for the price situation is the introduction of more money. We realize that we must hold the money stream in control until such time as excess production in this country, which otherwise would be wasted, requires a further supply of money. We say the line has to be held, however, and held scientifically until such time as that condition comes about wherein more purchasing power is needed.

One of the great weaknesses of the report brought in by the committee, as I read it, is its failure to divulge just what has been the effect of taxes upon prices. This matter of taxes has been engaging the attention of thinking men everywhere. Men are beginning now to pay much more attention to it than ever before. I have been interested in follow-
Report oj Prices Committee

ing what has -been done by one of the great advocates of an incentive system, supplying incentive by decent management-labour conditions, not only in order to increase the amount of production the people of -the country have to enjoy, but also to help bring down prices. I have in my hand a copy of a book called ""Lincoln's Incentive System"", by James F. Lincoln, president of a great electrical corporation in the United States. In this book the -writer outlines the details of a system his company has used, and indicates that lie has no labour-management troubles at all. Labour is satisfied; they have never had a strike. Year -after year, with the help of his employees Mr. Lincoln and his management have been able to effect new methods and procedures in manufacture that have resulted in -lower -prices to th-e consumers. But, as he points out, as these new methods have effected savings in costs that otherwise would :be passed on to the consumers, governments have come along and introduced taxation which more than made up for the savings effected by the new procedures and greater efficiency. Prices therefore were not reduced-, but rather went up.
I want to read just one or two short extracts to show what Mr. Lincoln thinks about this matter of taxation and- how it affects prices. First I refer to page 69:
It is safe to say that the present tax laws will he changed to encourage efficiency or we shall disappear as a great industrial nation.
That is the warning of a man who knows something about the effect of taxation upon production and prices. Again, at page 71 he says:

There must be a new approach to this matter of taxation. We must see it in its true relationship. Taxes are the greatest of all reducers of purchasing power. As a matter of fact, at this time taxes are largely the reason for much of the misunderstanding on wages between the industrial worker and his employer. The worker sees his standard of living going down. His only reaction is that his employer is not paying him enough since he cannot live as he did before. He is working as hard but is not enjoying the same kind of living.
Then to conclude this portion, at page 73 Mr. Lincoln says:

Perhaps the reader may feci that I am labouring this point of taxes and its relationship to the standard of living. I am not. The whole question of jobs, standard of living, industrial and human development, depends on our handling of this problem of the individual's relationship to his government. The answer that the American people give to this problem will determine not only the fate of incentive management but also their own. Serfdom and slavery we feel cannot happen here. However, taxation will accomplish the result as completely here as it has in countless cases in all history.

That ought to be a warning, it seems to me, to thinking people everywhere. If taxation is pushing up costs and is ruining the chances of the people to catch up with rising prices, then it seems to me that we ought to be doing something about it.

I should like to say a word or two in conclusion about incentive. If the cost of living is to be brought down to a reasonable level there must be high production and plenty of competition. Social C red iters believe in these two things, and in their effectiveness in stabilizing any economy. It stands to reason that if we are to have high production and plenty of competition, then there must be incentive to produce. Anything that will kill or destroy incentive has the effect of removing from the use of the people production which could be brought into being.

There are some in our country who advocate that the only way to deal with the present situation is through government ownership of the means of production and distribution. But the thing which always interests me about the claims of these people is that they never tell us what they will use for incentive. That is the dangerous part of the matter. You cannot get people to make an effort unless there is incentive, unless they think there is some personal reason why they should make an effort. And that reason is always associated with themselves and their own individual betterment.

Again I say, I should like to hear, just for once, what these people who advocate government ownership have to offer by way of incentive. We feel that there must be incentive, and one of the best ways to get incentive in production is to make government policies such that a larger percentage of the production of a man's own labour remains in his own hands for his own use or his own distribution. Where do profits stand in this incentive scheme of things? Let me make clear that we as Social Crediters have never made the claim that the sole aim and objective of the production effort should be profits. We recognize, however, that profits have their place in the scheme of incentive production. They do provide an incentive. But any time that we begin to make profits the sole aim and end of production, instead of the satisfactory use and distribution of the goods we produce, we begin to get ourselves into serious trouble.

However, Social Crediters do say that profits are an incentive and that, as such, in any free and responsible enterprise economy, profits must remain. We have no objection whatever to reasonable profits being used as an incentive to all-out production.

HERRIDGE (Kootenay West):,,QUESTIONS,MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE,,Mr. Speaker, when this debate commenced it was not my intention to speak, for I understood that two or three speakers were to present the views of the various parties and the debate would then conclude; but since it has continued at some length, and in view of some of the remarks which have been made, I have a few words to say.

When the appointment of the committee was being debated early in the session I expressed the opinion that such a committee was unnecessary, because the government had in the wartime prices and trade board and in the Combines Investigation Act all the machinery required to do the work the committee was being asked to do. I still hold that view. But now that the committee has sat, and I know its members have worked hard, although in the first instance it was not supposed to make recommendations, I am pleased to note that some recommendations have been brought before the house by the committee. That is something concrete at least for this house to discuss and to accept or reject.

I am not going to deal with the recommendations in detail. It is sufficient to say that, while they do not bring forward the ideas which many of us in this house have advocated in regard to over-all price control and subsidies, the recommendations, if given effect, will be of some benefit to the Canadian people. The very fact that these recommendations have been brought before the house by the committee is an indication that the government has its ear to the ground and is listening to some extent to the opinions of the Canadian people as expressed through many organizations, and as emphatically expressed during the recent by-elections. That is more than I can say for the Progressive Conservative party, which apparently never has its ear to the ground.
The recommendation concerning the taxation of unreasonable profits is a step in the right direction. The recommendation for
Report of Prices Committee

more flexible rental control regulations is also a step in the right direction. While I am a supporter of rental controls, I do think, because of the inflexible nature of rent controls, many home owners are today suffering an injustice. Therefore, while the report is not all I could wish it to be, I intend to support it, because I believe it holds some germ of good which may bring forth fruit satisfactory to the Canadian people if the government takes immediate action-and that is the important point.

I wish to refer to the remark made by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) that the C.C.F. was not the only party which had the welfare of the Canadian people at heart. He suggested that other parties had the people's welfare just as much at heart. In reply I would say that the C.C.F., in advocating price controls and subsidies, at least recognizes and attempts to reflect in this house the opinions of the Canadian people; for, as indicated by a recent Gallup poll, over seventy-four per cent of the Canadian people expressed a desire for the reimposition of price controls and certain subsidies on essential commodities. All the trade unions in Canada-all of them-have expressed a desire for the same thing. So have the co-operative organizations; so have women's organizations in large numbers. The Canadian Legion also, at its last annual convention, unanimously supported the resolution urging a rolling back of prices to the 1946 level, which would mean a restoration of price control.

Therefore I think the hon. member for Kamloops, in ignoring the wishes of the labour unions in his riding and of the co-operatives in his riding and of the women's organizations in his riding and of the branches of the Canadian Legion in his riding, all of whom have demanded the reimposition of price controls and subsidies on certain essential commodities, is the member who is living in a world of unreality, which I suggest, Mr. Speaker, will be dissolved in the next general election.

I say, too, that the party to which he belongs is living in a world of unreality. At this stage in the development of our social order, when people are looking forward to reforms and doing away with the iniquities of the past I say, and I say it in all kindliness because I believe they are sincere and fair in expressing their views, it is the party to which the hon. member for Kamloops belongs which is living in a world of unreality when it ignores the will of the people expressed so unanimously in favour of price controls and subsidies.
Similarly, when his party will also continue to oppose the imposition of the excess profits tax, will urge higher interest rates in this

country, and will defend the interests of the'1 grain exchange as against the interests of the Canadian wheat grower, it lives in a world of unreality. I admit the difficulties in regard to-price control in peacetime because of constitutional jurisdictions; but at least this report, with all its deficiencies, has attempted to make an approach to solving the problem, an approach which I think should be acceptable to all democratic interests concerned. It is not a negative report. It is a positive report, having in view the welfare of the Canadian people.

We are living in a changing world. I am one of those who believe that we are living in a world in which either we must have a measure of regulation and planning under capitalism, or we shall have chaos, and I am glad to note that this committee, and the government to the extent that they support the recommendations of the committee, recognize that either we must have some regulation of capitalism and some control of its worst features, or we shall have chaos. The report with all its limitations recognizes to some extent that fact. For the hon. member for Kamloops to talk of loss of freedom should this freely elected parliament act in the interests of the people in this direction is absurd in the extreme.

A week ago tonight, I think it was, we had this press report, this government by press release, if one may call it that. It prompted me to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbo'tt) a question, and it prompted him the following day to make this answer, which I think he must have given with some pain. He said as reported at page 5627 of Hansard:

It is most unusual for a minister of finance or any other minister either to confirm or to deny rumours of this kind. But in view of the widespread publicity which has been given to this rumour and the statement of my hon. friend I have no alternative but to say that the rumour is without foundation.

That was a nice position to put the Minister of Finance in, was it not? He had to say in this house last Tuesday that this rumour, which we now find out is perfectly true down to the last ""i"" and the crossing of the ""t"", was without foundation. I also want to associate myself fully with what was said by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), who said to the government that if things are to be done before the next parliament assembles the time to do them is now, and not after parliament prorogues. I want to take a very few minutes on this question of prices. It is so easy to allow our hearts to run away with our heads, and to refuse to think about this at all. It is easy to say that a lot of people want it and that, therefore, we must have it. I know a lot of people want it; but the question is whether the people who have been closest to it, tried to study it and know the most about it, think it will work. We would all like it. I would love to think we could have price control, and get everything down to the price where I could buy it and it would not do any harm. Of course I would like it, and I suggest that a great many of the seventy-four per cent, or whatever the figure was, of the people were really saying, ""We want the prices down"". Of course they want them down.
I want to look in a detached way if I can at the causes of high prices. There is no mystery about it. Some of them are the faults of the government and some are not.
I -hall try not to pretend that I think the government is at fault where I do not believe it is.

First of all, there are the gifts to Britain, which every man in this house approved. We gave hundreds of millions away because we thought our honour and interest demanded it, but we gave this money away and got nothing in return. That meant less goods for us, and in the meantime purchasing power was created. That is a cause.

Then, of course, the second cause is the enormous increase in the money supply, which has multiplied three times since 1939. Vast amounts of it went into goods that were destroyed during the war. We have three times as much money and nothing like three times as much goods. I will not take time to give the figures, but we have vastly less than three times as much goods and, I suspect, less than twice as much. And do not forget that the money is being freely spent.

Then we have the inflationary policy of the government, of which I have spoken in the house. I do not propose to take any more time in discussing that now. I wish, however, to mention particularly a matter that I have brought up before, and that is the colossal mistake made in the exaggerated, accelerated and, indeed, almost fantastic depreciation policy which was followed by the government, whereby in the last several years we have increased our productive capacity at a rate seven times as fast as they have been doing in the United States.
I come to another thing which is tremendously important and which I think we are

1542103,ca.proc.d.1948-06-28.2.6.60,1948-06-28,82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a,ca.m.8707,Mr. MACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontario):,,QUESTIONS,MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE,,I am not offering any comments on leisure, whether it is good or bad, but I am repeating that it costs money and this finds its way into the cost of living. We need not pretend that it does not. I have outlined the farmers' position and, I repeat, they have been getting too little for too long.

The next reason I should like to mention is taxation, and reference has already been made to that. I will not do more than refer to it casually. We all know the enormous amounts of taxation that we pay, and the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) spoke very well on that point this afternoon.
There is another thing I would mention. It is rather delicate to mention it, but I will do so just the same. We do not work as hard as we used to, even when we do work. That,

I believe, is true of a great many people. From the huge amounts of money created during the war we have got the idea that money and value do not depend directly upon work, that you can escape work and still get money in some way. That this feeling prevails is true, I believe, and I am not going to discriminate as between this one and the other. It is not confined to any section of the community. A
Report oj Prices Committee
young man goes into an office, a vigorous young man, and he hears, ""Don't work too hard"".

The next point I would touch upon is profiteering. I expect there is profiteering, though not nearly as much as some people believe; that is, people who are too fond of witch hunting. I believe that if the most extravagant critic of the capitalistic system in this house, provided that he were a reasonable man-and there are such men in this house- were to total up all the profits he considered excessive and to divide them over the cost of living he would find that it was but a fleabite, something infinitesimal. I believe that with all my heart.
Then, of course, there is the thing that has been mentioned here, reduction of supply, particularly of food, because of controls. I do not need to tell the farmers about that. They know all about it.

I am not suggesting that this can all be put upon the government. Quite a lot of it can, and the government should act. My hon. friend the member for Eglinton has pointed out how they should act. But a great deal of it does not depend upon them; it depends upon ourselves.

Let me reiterate for a moment what in my opinion the government can do. It can do, months late, what we on this side of the house- I believe, all on this side of the house-told them last December and January that they should do, when we pointed out to them that they ought not have put on these taxes. In their hearts they did not like them, but they got involved and they just put on the taxes. Then the hon. member for Eglinton pointed out again what we said at the time of the budget, that some relief should be given to people in the low-income group.

But I do not want to leave it there entirely; I want to come back to remedies which are in our own hands, because I do not think we want to leave it all to the government. We can do a great deal ourselves with a measure of self-discipline. Consumers can do a great deal by themselves. I do not want to be personal, but in my own family wre do not buy nearly as much high-priced meat as we used to. Some hon. members may say I am not a very good advertisement for the result; but, believe it or not, I have put on a pound or two.

There is another thing we people in the cities can do; I do not apply this to farm people at all. We can work harder; and if we work harder we shall have more goods and prices will come down. There is no mystery about prices.

But these remedies I have given, which we may apply ourselves, are awfully unattractive. No one wants to believe that a thing is his own fault, or that there is anything he can do about it. He wants to have some outside mechanism come in and do it all for him; and that is why controls are so popular. People think it can be all done by controls; and my hon. friend to the left, who spoke so well, pleaded that we should take a humanitarian view. I do not think it is taking a humanitarian view to refuse to think, or to suggest to people remedies you know will never work. I believe that is a cruel thing. I think it is cruel to suggest to the people remedies which will turn out to be no remedies at all.

Controls are terribly attractive. In the first place, they relieve us from doing anything ourselves. In the second place, and this is important, they make us feel that we are going to punish somebody. We feel that someone else is being naughty, and we are going to punish him. That is why people stumble into this sort of thing. Have they ever had this view from anyone who has had experience in controls and their exercise? I Shall, however, come to that later.

Of course we are all tired to death of hearing the record of controls during the war. On the whole it is a good record, though we must remember that part of it was quite illusory, because the low prices were supported by subsidies amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars. So we were paying out of one pocket what we saved for the other. Nevertheless I must admit that, in wartime, controls worked pretty well, and the government did a pretty good job. But can anyone point to any democratic country where, except under war emergency or its equivalent, that ""comprehensive system of controls"" advocated the other day iby the 'hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) has ever worked in peacetime? In England they have an emergency now far greater than in wartime; but even there the controls are creaking and crumbling; and the desperate difficulty they are in, in my opinion and in the opinion of the people much wiser than I, is at least partly due to the unwise application of controls. The newspaper I often quote, The Economist, is very wise, I think, in not putting all the blame on labour. If I remember rightly, the other day it said one of the difficulties in England was that capital and labour are both doing themselves pretty well, by which it meant that neither was stretching itself as much as it might.
My next point is this. I can understand people asking for controls; but I cannot understand people asking for controls and at
Report oj Prices Committee

the same time saying they will not have wage controls. To me that just does not click; it does not make sense. I do not understand how any reasonable man can say that; yet it is my understanding that this is just what many people who are advocating controls do say.

Now we come along to this wonderful phrase, ""rolling back prices,"" which has a kind otf biblical sound, like rolling back the soroll of the heavens, like Joshua making the sun stand still, though it was only for an hour. We have the demand to roll back prices. It sounds grand. ""Roll the old chariot along""; I think there is an old song to that effect. Let us have a look at this rolling back of prices. Let us hear the word of a man who knows something about it, a man who had) the job and did it well, Mr. K. W. Taylor. At page 87 of the proceedings of the prices committee he was asked, ""How about rolling back butter prices to the level of 1946? In your opinion what would be the result?"" And his reply was: ""Complete chaos."" Those were the words of Mr. Taylor, who was head of the prices board and who now is one of the assistant deputy ministers of finance. So there is the opinion of a man who has been working on this very thing. He has seen both sides. He is a sensible man. He knows more about it than any of the rest of us, and that is what he says. I think it is reasonable to ask the opinion of men of that kind.

I go further and say I do not think it is possible to adduce evidence of a single country which has had experience in the administration of these controls to show that we should have a comprehensive system of controls reimposed, which is what is being asked. I repeat that they 'have never worked in a democratic country in peacetime. It is a matter of common knowledge that when they were taken off officially in the United States, actually they were off already. The thing had1 become a joke; people just would not accept it, and partly at any rate they took off controls because they were practically off already. For us to suggest now that we are going to retrace our steps and impose over-all controls is just not reasonable. ""Hypocrisy"" is a nasty word and I shall not use it, but I just say that is a bit of the most utter unrealism I could possibly think of.

But do not take my view; do not even take the view of anyone who shares my opinions. Let us come to a witness who, I think, will be accepted by hon. gentlemen to the left. This instance has been mentioned already by the hon. member for Lake Centre; therefore I can pass over it quickly. Let us come to the

government of Saskatchewan and the instance we were given this afternoon of the fact that they had an act to enable them to control prices, which act they did not use. It was on the statute books for a year. That is where it should be; because after all, it is a purely provincial matter; but the act was allowed to lapse. Why did they not use it out there? The reason is simple. That is a province of farmers, people who are interested in getting good prices for their food products. But it was food prices that caused much of the trouble in Vancouver Centre, in Oshawa and elsewhere. So there you have a case of making the best of both worlds. We had the C.C.F. profiting-and I am not going to be too critical of them-from stressing inflated food prices in the industrial constituencies, and at the same time refraining from price control in Saskatchewan itself, for the obvious reason I have given. So I say it is a travesty to have a political party demanding in Ottawa, where they have no power, what they will not do in Saskatchewan, where they have the power.

I say that controls are not the answer, that controls will make confusion worse confounded. If I believed controls would do the job I would try to bring myself to accept them, even believing as I do that they would grievously hamper our freedom. But I am saved that, because I am perfectly satisfied that they will not work.

What is the answer, then? Well, I have really covered most of the things I wanted to say. The answer is to remove these absurd austerity taxes which never should have been imposed; which, as we have been reminded, we actually defeated in committee at one stage, though the defeat did not stick. Halt the various inflationary measures. These are the things government can do; but, as I said before, I am not going to put it all on the government, though there is a great deal the government should do now, without waiting for it to be done as a Christmas present after the convention in August, which I am very much afraid will be the case.

On the other hand, there should be harder work and more self-discipline on the part of people individually. If it would not sound like introducing sentiment at the end of a speech which certainly has not had much sentiment in it, I would say this. There was running through my mind this morning a jingle I remember seeing once in the army, where, as a matter of fact, many of us learned to work together in a way we have sometimes forgotten since. I am not sure that the idea expressed in this jingle has not a great deal
Report oj Prices Committee

to do with it. I thought it was by Kipling, but today I find it is not. I want to close with these words, because they indicate the kind of co-operation and working together which is necessary, along with all the things the government can do, instead of these precious controls which will not work:
It ain't the individual, nor the army as a whole;
But the everlastin' teamwork of every [DOT]bloomin' soul.
I suggest that is what we want, rather than witch hunts, together with the measures the government can take.

1542158,ca.proc.d.1948-06-28.2.6.115,1948-06-28,a519c7ba-e092-4c85-95fb-2519b2cbfc06,ca.m.8326,Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,QUESTIONS,MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE,,should be generally condemned when, as a matter of fact, only certain small sections of business have been proved to be guilty of so-called profiteering, if I may use the word, which would stand a lot of definition. One other observation with respect to these comments. One section of the report deals with matters which I understand were never before the committee at all.

We have this statement in the findings, if I may summarize it. It says that the significant causes of the rise in prices are four: first, the rise in external prices, the rise in prices outside this country; second, increases in the cost of producing certain goods; third, the expansion of purchasing power, and fourth, certain supplementary factors, which I presume include so-called profiteering. I shall touch briefly on these findings in a minute or two.

Nearly half of the so-called conclusions published in the report under fourteen different headings are criticisms of government policy in Which many sections of this house have taken part and are in substantial agreement, and in which I am sure many of those sitting to your right, Mr. Speaker, are in agreement as well. One-quarter of these findings are vague and, to-some extent, meaningless. They have been gone over by others. Several speakers have taken them one after the other and discussed them. I therefore do not propose to do that.

The third group of conclusions was referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) as being the ash-can- group of conclusion-recommendations which leave loopholes and possible delays for the government to follow or not to follow in dealing with this important matter.

With respect to the report itself, my first observation is that it is a most inadequate document, presuming to deal with what is perhaps the major economic question facing this country today. The committee was appointed to find the causes of these rising prices, and yet not the slightest attempt was made to examine the effect of the government's policies on these rising prices. We tried to have that as a requirement of the committee. By your ruling, Mr. Speaker, that was not allowed. In dealing with this problem, the effect of government policies during recent months and years was practically left out of consideration by the committee; government policies relating to taxation, to expenditures, to trade, to currency and credit were practically not considered at all. The objectives of the committee, and I think many of us think the objectives of the government, seem
to be to find some whipping-boy, some scapegoat on whom they can lay the blame for these unfortunate conditions in our economy.

Before I sit down I propose to show that the major blame for this price condition rests on government policies chiefly. The effort has seemed to be to leave the impression that somebody else was to blame for this condition. When we have a situation of this kind, such effects as these have some causes. Providence did not give us this price situation. In their individual or in their collective capacities, man gave it to us-perhaps nations helped. As I said, wherever there is such an effect there is a cause.

What is the cause of rising prices?. It is the situation where the Supply of goods is out of relationship to the supply of credit or currency. One can say that the remedy is to increase the supply of goods or to reduce credit or currency. I suggest that under these conditions our hands are tied. If we start out to try to reduce the credit or currency available here, what will happen to our national income? What will happen to our wage level? What will happen to our capacity to pay our debts? Nothing but harm. Therefore it leaves us with the other alternative of finding a way to increase production. I propose to deal with these matters in a little more detail later on.

But what I want to say now is this. This high price situation did not come about by accident; it had causes. What are these causes? That is what the people of Canada want to know, and how the condition can be remedied, nothing else. It is natural that those who are in positions of responsibility should try to leave the impression that others are to blame. But what we have to try to do is to find out what are the real causes and what are the best remedies that we can follow from now on.

In the report, four or five things are mentioned as being the chief contributing causes to this condition. One of them is foreign prices. No doubt the rise in prices elsewhere has been a factor; but I suggest., with all respect, that it has not been a major factor in the rise of prices in Canada. Another suggestion is that certain companies have sold their goods for what somebody was willing to pay; that the prices they received were considerably more than what they had paid and that profits were made. No doubt that has been true. Whether that is to be regarded as profiteering is a matter for examination.
I want to ask the house, is the man who today has some cattle on his farm to be regarded as a profiteer if he holds them off for a few weeks, in view of the fact that the

government of Canada is reported as likely to remove the embargo on cattle going to the United States? Is the man who grew oats and barley a year or two ago, and, on learning that the government was likely to remove the price ceiling on these commodities, to be regarded as a profiteer if he held his oats and barley until the government made its move and the price went up 50 per cent? Is he to be regarded as a profiteer who, under conditions where dominion policies increased the supply of currency and credit far beyond the supply of goods, thus ensuring a rise in prices, takes advantage of that situation? I am not answering that question; I am just raising it. If every such man is to be regarded as a profiteer I ask, who in Canada is innocent?

No doubt, profits have been made. Profits could not help but be made under conditions of inflation, where prices were sure to rise. The government had the alternative of trying to see that commodities equalled the amount of currency and credit or of bringing in and maintaining, if it could, an over-all policy of control.

The government has stated its position and we have stated ours. There is the constitutional aspect. There is also an economic aspect. Practically everyone today thinks that, under these conditions, that over-all kind of control policy could not be carried out, and would not produce results if it were, without wage controls. And if we have price controls and wage controls we must tell every worker where he has to work and how much he can get for what he does, as well as what will happen if he does not do what he is told. It is generally recognized now that such an over-all system would lead to communism, the one thing that nearly everyone in Canada is afraid of.

Certain evidence is brought forward to leave the impression that great profits were made. No one denies that profits were made. Everyone who had any physical goods found that their value went up, just as if prices were to go down they would lose. Prices went up and many made profits, and if prices went down they would lose. But certain evidence was brought forward, and I will give one item as an illustration. It is said that cocoa beans increased in price 283 per cent. I have not checked it, but I have no doubt that is the fact. But what is the bearing of that on the cost of living? I am told only that 1-6 ounces of this commodity is used by the average family in Canada each week, so that even if that statement represents a fact, which I do not question, it has little bearing on the practical question of how to control prices
that are 50 per cent higher than they were before the war; wholesale prices double what they were before the war.

The question of butter has been raised. Does anybody here question that, so far as butter is concerned, its costs have risen rapidly under recent conditions? If anyone doubts that suggestion, then I think he should look at the situation today. We have a price ceiling on butter and I suggest that we ask ourselves this question. With that price ceiling, is anybody in Canada at this time of the year, when production is high, going to buy butter at a fixed price and pay the storage and then be subject to a fixed price later on? That has been the common practice in normal times, because butter is produced in the summertime in larger quantities than in the winter. It looks as though now, under existing circumstances, there will be less butter next winter than there was last.

That, I suggest, will be a most unfortunate situation in view of the controversy between butter producers and those who would bring oleomargarine into the country. If we run into a further difficult situation in regard to butter next winter, part of the blame will lie on those who have put butter in the position it occupies today.

Two or three other things were said by the committee, one of which was that increases in cost of production were a cause of rising prices. Certainly they were; but what we want to know is, what contributed to the increased cost of production? We know some things that did so contribute; but what we do not know, and what the committee has not examined, is the result of government policies on the increasing costs of production. That, the committee has not reported upon, and that, the committee should have reported upon.

The report suggested that another cause of rising prices is increased purchasing power. That, too, is correct, but what contributed to the increased purchasing power? Some factors that contributed to it were laudable, things that we all want. Some other factors may not have been so laudable. What part had government policy in increasing purchasing power, and to what extent can it be justified? That, the committee did not answer; that, the committee should have answered.

Then the impression is left that the work of the committee, the examinations that took place under it, have struck terror into the hearts of businessmen, and that, because of that, good has been done and will continue to be done. That self-praise, in the face of the facts, is a poor recommendation for the committee.
Report of Prices Committee

What has been happening since the committee has been at work? The cost of living has gone up. and I venture the prediction that it has not stopped going up. Today, it is at 153-3, higher than we have ever before known it, higher than it was after the first war, during which, as someone said this afternoon, we did not have the controls we had in this second war, and certainly did not have the experience of a previous war, as we had in the last war.

What I wish to do today is to examine the effect of government policy on rising prices and to assess the degree of that effect; because frankly, in my judgment, government policy has had more to do with rising prices than all other factors put together, and yet it has not been examined by this committee.

On February 2 last I warned the government that Canada was facing the greatest economic problems the country had ever before been called upon to face. I predicted then that, because of the government's refusal to take effective action, the cost of living would increase beyond levels reached in the disastrous inflation of the nineteen-twenties. Events hnve now justified these warnings.

Prices in Canada now stand at by far the highest level in our history. The general cost of living index stands at 153-3, the clothing index at 173-6 and the food index at 191-6, nearly double pre-war, and still rising. And even these official indices, which are based on a subsistence standard of living and in many respects are not fair, do not reflect the actual burden borne by the average Canadian family.

The true position is more nearly reflected in the wholesale price index which, when computed on the same basis as the cost of living index, now stands, not at 153 but at 220. On this basis the average price of all commodities is well over twice the pre-war figure.

People are facing a situation in which it is becoming increasingly difficult to provide for themselves the necessities of life. I mentioned the wholesale price index, because we commonly quote the other figure. One is 153 and the other is 220. For this rise in prices the blame lies largely at the door of the government.

The government cannot excuse itself by saying that we are suffering from the aftermath of war. Of course the war created problems; but the people of Canada pay, in their heavy taxes, the expensive price of government in order to have these problems faced and overcome. Yet at almost every stage the policies of the government have heightened inflation and increased the burdens of the people.

The sole action taken by the government has been to appoint a committee of parliament to inquire into the cause of the rise in prices. This was sheer evasion and subterfuge. Everyone in Canada who had studied the matter knew why prices were rising. We had too little consumer goods. Why? Because the government encouraged reckless capital goods purchases in the United States; because they needlessly imposed embargoes on foods and goods from sterling area countries; and because they maintained at a high level a most regressive system of indirect taxes, such as the excise tax and the sales tax. Our dollar is worth only sixty cents, or perhaps only fifty cents, because the government doubled the money supply in comparison with the goods the nation produced, and because so much government expenditure was made on borrowed money, money borrowed by the government from the banks and not wholly from the public.

These are among the real causes of our inflation. The government alone is responsible for them and their ill consequences upon the people; and it has done its discreditable best to conceal what it did. Vagueness and confusion exist all through this country. There has not been the frank analysis of this situation that there should have been.

Let us look at the government's taxation system. What is the position? Before the war we spent $500 million a year. In the middle of the war we spent six times that, or around $3,000 million a year. What has happened since the war? Even in the present budget we are spending $2,700 million. The government increased our taxes by 500 per cent; then they reduced them by ten per cent. That is not the worst of it; there are two features which are particularly bad, not only the heavy burden but the proportion the government takes of all we make. Before the war this government took from the people of Canada ten per cent of all that everybody made. That is what the cost of government took from the pockets of the people. Now they are taking over twenty per cent of all everyone makes. If this keeps on in this country we shall foe in the position of trying to bring prosperity by each taking in the other's washing; when what we need is more instead of fewer people at productive work.

Canadian taxation is characterized by two features: 'taxation which bears unequally upon the poor, and taxation which taxes people when they do not know it. I refer to such indirect taxes as the excise and sales taxes. I am not suggesting that they could all be taken off. But those hidden taxes take out of the pockets of -the people of Canada $1,000
Report oj Pnces Committee

million that they do not know about. These taxes fall directly upon production', unlike other taxes which are imposed after the money is made. They increase the cost of living. They force down living standards. They hamper enterprise and restrict income and employment. It is true that last December, following criticism by myself and others, the government removed the sales tax on certain articles of food; but that is only a single step forward on a very long road. The sales tax remains on many materials and much equipment going inito the production of food and on all other consumer goods, as well as upon the instruments of their production.

The burden of these taxes has been great for many years, but last November the government added a special excise tax of 25 per cent to all the other indirect taxes. This additional tax applies to a long list of miscellaneous articles, such as automobiles, refrigerators, brushes, mirrors, cosmetics, combs, cameras and film, radios, toasters, food choppers, electric kettles, irons, vacuum cleaners and so on. Most of these and many more are rightfully regarded by the average Canadian family as part of the necessary equipment for living; yet the government imposed this special tax which increased costs, increased prices and further stimulated inflation.

I shall touch upon some half dozen other government policies and try to show how they have made this price situation worse. The second factor in creating inflation iwas the process of decontrol. The way these things were done almost looked as though their very purpose was to produce inflation. Of course that was not the intention, but we can see now what the consequences have been.

The' first step, away back in 1943, was the removal of subsidies on the production of certain essential goods. As the subsidies were removed, the marginal producers of essential goods, caught as they were between rising costs on the one hand and price controls on the other, were forced out of production, or compelled to concentrate on the most expensive lines.

The second major move along the line of decontrol was when the government, after t>wo or more years of subsidy removal, in 1945 began to remove price controls. All too often they began at the wrong end. By removing price controls from non-essential, capital and luxury goods first of all, they directed the nation's productive capacity into those lines, to the detriment and reduction of essential production. So by the end of the program the government had achieved the
maximum possible reduction of goods which are the essentials of life; and now have the effrontery to ask a committee of parliament to find out why the cost of living has gone up.
