,Progressive Conservative,,John Bracken,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a519c7ba-e092-4c85-95fb-2519b2cbfc06&Language=E&Section=ALL
1542159,ca.proc.d.1948-06-28.2.6.116,1948-06-28,a519c7ba-e092-4c85-95fb-2519b2cbfc06,ca.m.8326,Mr. BRACKEN:,Leader of the Official Opposition,QUESTIONS,MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE,,Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was dealing with the report of the committee with reference to the rise in the cost of living and prices generally. I had touched briefly upon the history of this matter from the time when the resolution providing for the setting up of the committee was passed, and I had dealt briefly with some of the findings of the committee. At that moment I was engaged in a discussion of certain of the government's policies, and their effect upon rising prices. And in this last respect I had dealt with two of those policies, namely taxation, and the manner in which the government had taken off certain of the controls.

I was about to deal with a third question of government policy, namely the expansion of credit. Apparently the government felt that inflation was not moving rapidly enough, so they helped in worsening the situation by increasing the bank-note issue to the extent of $25,000,000. Then they allowed credit expansion to proceed almost unchecked. Bank loans and investments increased by 8777 million over a short period. The net increase in capital stock issue was 8236 million in the same period, and corporate bonded debt increased by 881,000,000. The net result has been that the government's policies have given us less than half as much increase in production as they have given in expanded credit and currency. That is one of the chief causes of rising prices; and for it the government is wholly responsible.

Then, as if this were not enough, the government undertook a fourth measure, the most inflationary measure possible for any government to take, the heavy cash subsidization of new capital investment. Between November 10, 1944, and March 31, 1947, the government, through the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, extended special facilities to industrial investment through the allowance of double depreciation against income tax. This resulted in new investments totalling SI,200 million, against which tax abatements are estimated to have amounted to $220 million in 1947. This is the equivalent
Report of Prices Committee

of a cash subsidy of $220 million in rebates in taxation to encourage commercial investment. It thereby took from those who would use certain of these commodities, lumber, cement and other things, goods to the value of $1,200 million. It thus lessened the amount of these goods available for other purposes, thereby permitting or encouraging increases in cost.

This subsidizing of commercial construction and investment, in a time of acute shortage of consumer goods, greatly intensified the general inflation. This increased the cost of housing immediately; it increased the price of commodities beyond the reach of the average individual, and these increases extended all through the entire range of goods and services in current use. The view of the Progressive Conservative party is that, although capital investment is most desirable and quite essential to our long-term welfare, the government was paying subsidies to this extent out of public funds at a time when it would cause great hardship to the people at large.

We now come to the fifth of the government's policies, their trade policy. After having imposed unparalleled pressure on the limited supply of goods available, supplies which were limited largely as a result of government policy, they proposed to shut off a wide range of these supplies for the purpose of saving dollars. But many imports required not a single United States dollar in connection with their purchase from sterling area countries. Some of these embargoes were totally unnecessary, but they are the reason why such articles as tomatoes-I give that as one example- have been sold in Ottawa for as high as eighty-four cents a pound.

But the government, apparently not being satisfied with the mischief they had already wrought, undertook yet another measure, the reimposition, on January 1 last, of a long schedule of customs duties against the remaining imports which they permitted the citizens of Canada to obtain in the sterling area. As a result, prices once more marched upward toward infinity. I wish to make it quite clear that all these restraints on our trade with the British commonwealth had nothing to do with the dollar crisis, but they had much to do with aggravating the living crisis of Canadians.

In the face of these numerous actions by the government, all of which have increased inflationary pressures, the remarkable fact concerning prices is that they are not twice as high as they are, that the wholesale price index does not stand twice as high as it is-at 440 instead of 220. That the situation is not worse is a tribute to the patriotism, good sense and selfrestraint of all sections of our economy-of business people, of labour, and, above all, of
the average Canadian. Had it not been for this, the ill results of these government policies would have been much greater than they are.

In distressing and perplexing times such as these, it is the tendency of all of us to seek a panacea-some one, simple solution of all our troubles. Many have been led to believe that in the price control such a panacea was to be found. Our experience in the war, under the dictatorial powers given the government over prices and wages, laid the basis of that idea. For this false conception, as applied in peacetime, the government is alone to blame; because all during the war it constantly led the people to believe that price controls were, in fact, such a panacea; that price controls were the simple answer to the problem of how to fight a world war without any inconvenience at home. As usual, this kind of government propaganda misled if it did not deceive the people.

The government, by such politically conceived propaganda-I use that term in no ulterior sense, because it was their privilege to sell the idea of price control in wartime; my criticism is that it was overdone and the impression left with everybody in Canada that the same kind of thing could be carried on in peacetime, with equally good results, and when it was not carried on and prices did go up as they have gone up, then came the public reaction and the people said, ""You did it before; you said you would do it again; you have not done it; therefore we will spank you""-created the illusion which for a while concealed the true nature and effect of the government's wartime policy. Now that illusion has been cruelly shattered. Not even the socialists and communists are sufficiently naive to believe that price control without wage control can ever counteract the effect of the multitude of inflationary measures which have been put to work by the government.

A little before six o'clock the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) mentioned two things. He referred to something I was reported as having said about the attitude of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Miller) toward price control. I think what was said was that his views with respect to the price controls were not different from those of the government. I think he said that and I may have repeated what he said. What the hon. member for Dauphin also said was that price controls were only a palliative, that they were not a permanent long-term remedy for this situation. With that we all agree.
What, then, is the situation now? A frustrated public now asks, what are we to do? The first thing we must do is to put an end
Report oj Paces Committee

to this business of skidding from crisis to crisis, snatching first at one expedient and then at another. Palliatives will not and cannot remove the causes of the present inflation. We must find ways to prevent the present so-called crisis from becoming a permanent condition of our economic life. We must find ways to prevent the minister's austerity program from becoming the permanent pattern for the life of Canada. Only positive remedial action will do that.

We must, first of all, set out to get rid of much of the welter of indirect taxes which are everywhere increasing the cost of production, and the cost of living, as well as restricting income and employment. The first to go must be the long list of 25 per cent excise taxes which were imposed by radio broadcast on November 18 last. The next to go must be the sales tax, in so far at least as that item enters into the cost of living. There must be reductions in the income taxes paid by people who do not make enough on which to live.

Perhaps I might be permitted to intrude another thought here. I sometimes wonder how we get in a state of mind that under postwar conditions like this we can all expect to have higher incomes, higher wages, help rebuild other nations and provide more generously for social security; how we expect to do all that and at the same time pay $2,700 million in taxes and still not have higher prices, is hard to understand. There has been something wrong with our thinking somewhere. We cannot rehabilitate Europe; we cannot add to our own well-being; we cannot pay higher taxes without either increasing production or doing with less. That is basic in our approach to this problem.

If we are to help over there, it is not bookkeeping; it is not dollars; it is not a manipulation of our currency-it is goods that will help. If we are to send them more than we have sent in the past we shall have to produce more than we have produced in the past or do with less ourselves. But there seems to be an inclination to produce less, and there is not much inclination to do with less.

Next, we must consider seriously the removal of many of the embargoes, quotas and tariffs which are shutting off our imports from the United Kingdom and other parts of the sterling area. We have been sending goods over there; they are unable to pay for them all, and in some respects we have been making it difficult or impossible for them to pay for them by shutting out more than we did during the war the goods that they could send in here. These restrictions have been
creating artificial scarcities and forcing up consumer prices here in Canada.

It is time that everyone in Canada realized that if these artificial restrictions could be removed we could get ourselves in due course into a much more fortunate position in the world as far as helping forward both ourselves and our less fortunate brethren in Europe are concerned.

Finally, we must overtake the government's inflation of our currency by greater productions. As a distinguished United States scholar and statesman, Bernard M. Baruch, said recently, ""Production, production, production -that is the law and the prophets."" We here in Canada also must realize the importance of production. To that end the government must get off the taxpayer's back by lessening taxes; business must set out to produce more without an increase in profit; labour must increase its productivity without an increase in wages; and. finally, farmers must plan to produce more without increased income. In addition, all of us, including the government, must learn that wars once fought have to be paid for, and that they can be paid for, destroyed nations rehabilitated, and high standards of living maintained, only if, by the partnership of us all, we produce more of the essential goods needed for the human family to live on.

If the government fails in its task, as it is doing, and if the rest of us prove to be unwilling to make these comparatively minor sacrifices we shall deserve our fate, another depression. But the government must give the lead. It must get off the backs of the people, instead of putting heavier burdens upon them.

If, then, we have the courage, the vision and the tenacity to face our problems, and then to work with a will to carry them out, we shall find that our price troubles will commence to disappear. But they will vanish only when we do two things: first, when we all learn that production is the only thing that will save us and that production means work by us all and, second, when the government refrains from its customary practice and puts economically sound instead of political expedient policies into effect. As I have tried to point out, the government has gone the wrong way about some of these matters. A reversal of its taxation and production plans is long overdue.

With many of the sections of this report we are in agreement; but, as a means of meeting the problem of rising prices, we consider that it is evasive, incomplete and less than frank with the Canadian people. We are not opposed, as I said, to many of the so-called recommendations or conclusions in this
Report oj Prices Committee

report. What we are opposed to is what has been left out of the report, namely, a consideration of the effect upon prices of the government's own inflationary policies. We are opposed to what the government has left out of the report more than we are to what it contains.

Some of our suggestions were outlined in our amendment, and I have tried to make a fuller statement upon them in my remarks tonight. Because of the inadequacy of the report for the purpose intended, we shall vote against it.

1542160,ca.proc.d.1948-06-28.2.6.117,1948-06-28,62287d4a-32a2-4734-a1b3-18cce52da443,ca.m.5390,Mr. CLARENCE GILLIS (Cape Breton South):,,QUESTIONS,MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE,,Mr. Speaker, I had not intended taking part in this debate; but, after listening to some of the statements recently made, it is necessary, even at the risk of keeping the house here for a day or so longer, that the house and the country should have a clear understanding of the basis of the present debate.

The question before us is, in my opinion, the one that is uppermost in the minds of the Canadian people, namely, why there has been such a shrinkage since 1945 in their purchasing power or real wages. While the reason may be clear to many of us in this house, I am fairly sure that it is not clear to some of the speakers this afternoon and this evening, whose remarks may tend to confuse some people in this country.

What is the issue? The issue is that the government and the official opposition, by the removal of the controls which protected the consuming public of Canada during the war period, initiated a movement which in effect has robbed the people of from 30 to 40 per cent of their real income since 1945. Has that actually happened? The answer is yes, and the proof of the fact that there is something wrong with our price structure is that the government of Canada and the House of Commons saw fit to appoint a special committee which has spent several months in taking evidence to determine what is wrong in our economy. The report of that committee is now before us.

The first fact to be established is that there is something wrong with our economy. The committee's report is proof positive of that. But before going into the subject matter of the report, just to set the record straight I understood the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) to state this afternoon that the C.C.F. group in this house had supported amendments to the 25 per cent excise tax.
I stated that he was not present when this group forced the vote on the abolition of the 25 per cent excise tax. To be fair to the hon.
member, on the assumption that he wants to be fair to us, I wish to say that the hon. member for Lake Centre was present in the house.

1542232,ca.proc.d.1948-06-28.2.6.189,1948-06-28,62287d4a-32a2-4734-a1b3-18cce52da443,ca.m.5390,Mr. GILLIS:,,QUESTIONS,MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE,,You objected to it this afternoon and tried to imply that, as far as the C.C.F. are concerned, they were advocating directed labour and all that kind of nonsense.

With regard to the report itself, when the proposal was made to set up a committee the C.C.F. took the position that it should not be set up, that it was the responsibility of parliament to do something about price levels. Our view was that this was our job in the House of Commons, and we voted against the setting up of a committee. Nevertheless we bowed to the will of the majority, and when the House of Commons decided that a committee would be set up we appointed members to serve on it. Those members took their place in the committee and discussed the question during the deliberations of the committee. The report of the committee was brought into the house and our assumption is that it is merely another report. We believe the report will be tabled in the House of Commons and relegated to the archives. I hope it will not be, but that has been the history of past reports.

We have tried to amend the report, asking the house to refer it back to the committee. We have sought to have the committee revived for the purpose of amending the report by doing certain specific things immediately, such as the reimposition of the excess profits tax and some measure of controls and the establishing of subsidies. Our proposal was ruled out of order. We are in a position now where we are faced with a vote on this report, and I will say this about it. I have read the report and, if it means what it says, there is a certain amount of meat in it. If the tabling of the report means that the government will take this report and do something about the fourteen recommendations made by the committee, all of which are good if they are acted upon-though we are still suspicious that they will not be acted upon-and if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the other ministers charged with the responsibility for government policy intend to do these three things, as far as this group is concerned we will vote for the report. There is something in it; it is a step in the right direction. We are assuming that the government will do something about it, and on those grounds we are quite prepared to support the recommendations of the committee.

I want to conclude by making an appeal to the official opposition. I do not know whether they mean what they say; but this afternoon, for example, the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell)-another man for whom I have a great deal of respect, and of whom I knew something a good many years ago, when he did not know anything about me, back when he was with the Eastern Trust Company-made a statement in reply to a question by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine). He said that profits were legitimate, that there was nothing wrong with them; and he quoted a book he hadi read, the author of which I know. The hon. member said if it is fair for labour to ask for certain increased wage rates, which is profit, then it is as reasonable for capital to have a profit on its investment.

The two points are entirely separate and distinct. Invested capital has no right to earn profit. Wages is something that accrues from the sweat and labour of a human being who stands for eight or ten hours a day wrestling with the soil or with the tools of production. That person requires at least sufficient to maintain a home and provide for a family. At no time in the history of this world has that labourer, who wrings a living either from the soil or from the machinery of production, been overpaid. He has never been in the position
Report oj Prices Committee

where he could maintain his family in decency and comfort, let alone save something. To compare him with the man who has a million or two million dollars to invest, and who can sit back in comfort in a luxurious home and draw from investments the equivalent of the wages paid that labourer, is simply not a fair comparison. That is unearned increment.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me tell the government that if they were prepared to do three things I am sure all the members of this group would be prepared to go out and fight with them, and help them to get the public to understand. First, I think they *have to re-establish the excess profits tax. The profits of practically every corporation in Canada today indicate that they have more than they are entitled to. Then, if you took the money you extracted by means of the excess profits tax-and mind you, no one would go on relief because you took it; no one would be hurt as a result-you could apply it to subsidies on essential commodities such as foodstuffs, on which ninety per cent of the income of the workers is spent today, with prices at present levels. Then you should revise the policy announced by the government, and re-establish the machinery of the wartime prices and trade board. You could call it what you like. You need not call it the wartime prices and trade board; you might call it a stabilization organization, or anything else. Do these three things and, in my opinion, within the next six or eight months-it will not happen overnight-the government will be able to get this country on some kind of even keel.
You will have opposition from over here among the Tory party; make no mistake 5849-3821

about that. There will be plenty of opposition from them, because in my opinion-and I do not mean any disrespect to hon. members, because I think they are all pretty good fellows-they are managed from the outside by those who want a continuation of the machine that exploits the people of this country. That machine is gone, and the government should recognize it. We will support this report, and we expect the government to do something about it. Then, when you get in hot water with the Tories and big business on the outside, I think we shall be able to explain to the Canadian people the necessity for the action you have taken, whether or not it means anything to us politically.

PAUL MARTIN (Minister of National Health and Welfare):,Minister of National Health and Welfare,QUESTIONS,MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE,,Mr. Speaker, it is only appropriate that, as chairman of this committee, I should conclude the debate and try to meet as many as possible of the points which seem to me to be of special significance and which have been raised by those who have participated in the debate thus far.

I am sure the house would think I was only doing my duty if I were to pay tribute to all the members of the prices committee, regardless of party, for the great industry and diligence they have manifested since they were assigned the task given them in the middle of February last. Every member of the committee is deserving of the thanks of the House of Commons and of the people of Canada for the work they have tried to do in connection with this extremely difficult problem. And in paying tribute to them, I think it is only fair to include those agencies, such as press and radio, which have made known to the public the character and nature of the evidence being adduced by the committee through the interrogation carried out by two counsel who, as the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) said, have rendered distinguished service to the committee.

In assessing the merits of the committee, I think it is important to bear in mind why it was set up. It was set up primarily for the purpose of enabling members of the House of Commons to examine government officers, trade witnesses, and others, in order to see what light could be obtained in regard to this very difficult problem. It was basically a fact-finding committee and anyone who suggests, as did the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), that while this committee sat there was a rise in prices, and that the committee failed to do its job because it did not check inflationary tendencies, certainly is attributing to a parliamentary com-
Report of Prices Committee

mittee a power which any reasonable man in good judgment knows lies outside the scope and reach of a parliamentary committee. No one for a moment attempted to use this committee as a means of reducing the cost of living.

1542257,ca.proc.d.1948-06-28.2.6.214,1948-06-28,dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83,ca.m.8658,Mr. MARTIN:,Minister of National Health and Welfare,QUESTIONS,MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE,,The committee was used as a basis for determining what were the facts and to suggest remedial measures. Hon. gentlemen and others in the country said that there were profiteers in the country, that there were people who were hoarding, that there were people who were making profits away beyond any reasonable level; and it was because of the temper of the public mind and of parliament at that time that this committee was set up to try objectively to ascertain exactly what the situation was and what suggested steps the house and the government could take.

Having said that, I believe the fact is that the committee has had, as the hon. member for Cariboo said, a salutary effect. Among those witnesses called before the committee was Mrs. Marshall, head of the Canadian association of consumers. Speaking for thousands of women throughout this country, what was the nature of her evidence? She said that she looked upon this committee and, indeed, so did the members of her organization, as a fact-finding body that could, independent of that purpose, have a salutary effect. Indeed she said that at the time, when we were examining the cost of bread, it did have a salutary effect; for, while we were examining the question of the rise in bread prices, the evidence with regard to the ten-cent loaf of bread did have the effect of encouraging throughout the country a wider interest in and a greater amount of purchases of the lower-priced bread than of the higher-priced. This, together with the evidence of Doctor Pett of the Departmental of National Health and Welfare, as to the equivalent or better value from a nutritional standpoint of the ten-cent bread-again using the language of Mrs. Marshall-has had a salutary effect.

While the committee was still sitting, we had one gentlemen who has a series of stores in the city of Montreal announce to the committee that, because of its request, and because of the disclosure of his profit and loss figures, he proposed to reduce the cost of bread.

Then there was the evidence of the gentleman who said that if the committee were not sitting he would raise the price of bread; and there was another witness, during the later stages of the sittings of the committee who said, with regard to textile goods, that if the
committee were not sitting he would raise the prices of some of the articles manufactured by his company.

And so one could go on to indicate that there were salutary effects which emanated from the kind of information disclosed and the realization that corporations and others would be brought before the committee to give an account of the price situation as it applied to their particular business. But it is not fair to suggest, as did the leader of the opposition, that this report brands industry as a whole. I call the attention of the leader of the opposition to conclusion 14 of the report, in which the committee says:
Since the war, industry in Canada has been making commendable efforts to relieve these shortages.

Where industry had done its job, we were not hesitant to say it had done its job. There is no judgment on industry as a whole which would justify the leader of the opposition, or anyone else, in saying that this committee conceived of industry in its entirety as acting contrary to the public interest.

We appToached our task, and it was a difficult one, as men who, regardless of political affiliations, were anxious to know the facts of the case, in the knowledge that the possession of such information would be of great value. The house will recall that the committee did not delay in beginning its sittings because, no sooner had the house passed the resolution authorizing its establishment, than within a few hours the committee held its first session. I said to the committee at our first meeting:

The character of this committee will be determined by the members of this committee, and I am sure that they will not permit it to be used as a smoke-screen. They will not permit it to be a means of delaying action. In saying that the facts must be exposed, we should bear in mind that we are not a white-washing committee; nor, on the other hand, should this committee be used to ""smear"" anyone. This is a fact-finding committee. Our findings will, we trust, have a salutary effect, but no one who has acted fairly in setting prices need fear this investigation. But we should act without fear or favour, and I know that we will.

I know every hon. member of this committee will agree that, after allowance is made for the odd exception here and there, exceptions to which we all in some way or another contributed, that was the underlying principle by which, for the most part and generally speaking, every member of the committee sought to meet the assignment that had been given.

I can only say that perhaps the best judges of the work of the committee are the members of the committee themselves. While the hon. member for Cariboo does not think we have gone far enough in the conclusions, he said in
Report of Prices Committee

this house the other night-I compare his words with those of some others in his group-that this committee was a good committee; that it did the job assigned to it and, in so far as the conclusions met in part his point of view, he could not help but give it his support. I am mot using any part of the tributes or estimates made by any hon. -member on this side of the house; I am taking the comments of the hon. member for Cariboo, who, I think everyone on the committee will agree, was an extremely diligent member.

What did the committee basically conclude? The committee -had a whole series of witnesses before it. We had the evidence of the chairman of the wartime prices and trade 'board, of the governor of the Bank of Canada, of the head of the bureau of statistics, of the commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act; we had a series of other officials of the government, and I could not help but think, as those gentlemen were giving their evidence, of the plea made toy the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) in this house a year ago when he asked the government to set up a committee to investigate and interrogate officers of the -public service on -this and related questions. This government and this house gave the very thing the hon. gentleman asked for, and it is as a -result, in part, of what officers of the crown testified, that we are reporting to this House of Commons.

After the evidence was taken, we met and drew up our report and tried to arrive at what we thought would be the kind of commentary we should make about the problem generally and what we as a committee thought might be done to alleviate the severity of the problem.

I think the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) has taken a most unusual position in this debate. All through its deliberations he said that the committee was futile, that it was a waste of time, although I must say that he attended regularly and made valuable contributions toward some of its results. But I do not think I overstate the case when I say that he and his colleagues repeatedly took the position that the whole thing was a waste of time.

Yet when we came to the point in the final hours of the last meetings of the committee to try to see what we could recommend to our colleagues in this House of Commons and to the government of this country, what did we find? We found that not only was the hon. gentleman the only member of his party present when the conclusions were discussed and decided upon-

1542393,ca.proc.d.1948-06-28.2.6.350,1948-06-28,244e5dd5-8204-499b-b3f4-e73e59016198,ca.m.5191,Mr. McCANN:,Minister of National Revenue,QUESTIONS,MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE,,This government office economies control division was established in 1942 to examine and review all requests in public service for printing, stationery, office equipment and furniture before purchases are made. In general the terms and regulations embodied in P.C. 4428 and amendments
Supply-National Revenue
thereto are applied. Administration is centred in the director, whose duty it is to determine the necessity for the articles requisitioned, as also the quantity involved.

While records are maintained showing the number of requisitions dealt with and the estimated saving in each instance as a result of revision, any attempt to show by figures the economies effected in monetary value would not give the full amount, as no indication could be given recurrent savings.

In addition, to screening requisitions received each day, a careful review has been made of over 12,000 printed forms in use in the departments of the public service, and through substitution, lower grade quality of papers, standard size cut of forms, considerable initial and recurrent savings have been effected.

All free mailing lists in the departments of government have been curtailed to a minimum. Standardization of qualities Of paper in public printing and re-use of envelopes many times over have been effected, as well as reduction in qualities of binding of periodicals, publications, et cetera.

Careful review is made of all requisitions for publications, journals and other printed periodicals required for use of departments and approval confined to periodicals and scientific journals of use only to departments and libraries of government.

Periodic inspection is made of all government stores at Ottawa to ensure that stock is properly shelved and kept in clean and good condition. Inspection is also made of duplicating sections of departments of government and examination made of qualities of papers used on duplicating machines; furtherance of single space and narrow margin on copy and elimination of waste of paper and inks, et cetera, maintained.

Considerable study has been given by the director to the advisability of having dormant records microfilmed, so as to save the purchase of filing cabinets and space entailed in the filing and storage of dormant and semidormant files, and all departments have been advised accordingly. Several departments have adopted this process, and from information and records gathered it is believed that many other departments iwill follow.

1542403,ca.proc.d.1948-06-28.2.6.360,1948-06-28,244e5dd5-8204-499b-b3f4-e73e59016198,ca.m.5191,Mr. McCANN:,Minister of National Revenue,QUESTIONS,MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE,,The estimate submitted shows a slight increase in estimated expenditure for 1948-49 as compared with 1947-48. The amount for 1948-49 is $1,786,500. The increase is caused, first, by proposed staff appointments; second, proposed expansion of service; and third, necessary transcription service. With regard to the proposed increase in staff appointments, this ds particularly applicable to the European section, and the need for it can be understood by a reading of the statement included in the appended- notes at the end of this budget.

Briefly, the situation is that in some sections of our service we are able to secure to good advantage material for programs from freelancers. In other sections this is not the case. In the United Kingdom section, for instance, a great deal of free-lance material is available and is used. Such material is not equally available in the European section, since there are not a large number of free-lance writers with the necessary language qualifications available in Canada and, when they can be found, the fees charged for their work are very high. This makes it increasingly necessary to have in our European section staff members who are capable of producing their own material in the languages required.

Regarding the expansion of service, we anticipate that this will take place during the remainder of the period 1947-48 and in 1948-49. When the 1947-48 estimates were prepared, an increase in service was envisaged, namely the opening of a broadcast service to South Africa, Australasia, Belgium, Russia and Latin America. Only part of these plans has to this date been realized. We have established daily service in Spanish to Latin America. A halfhour program weekly is now transmitted to Australasia. We have made some test transmissions to South Africa. At present active consideration is being given to -the establishment of a regular service to Russia. Consideration is being given also to the advisability and the feasibility of service to South Africa and to Belgium in both French and Flemish. If these additional services are established
and certainly some of them will be-there will be a considerable increase in staff. This increase has been provided for in the budget estimates presented herewith.

As regards transcription service, it is to be noted that there is an increasing demand for and use of Canadian program material for relay over foreign broadcasting stations. The cost of making transcriptions is high, and therefore a separate amount is included in this budget under the ""performers' fees"" item to cover the requirements of this important service.

I might give the committee a little information in reference to this international short wave. Our physical plant is in Sackville, New Brunswick. It was built in 1942 and is owned outright by the crown, but is operated for a fee by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. No licence fees are collected from anybody with respect to international short wave; all the expenses come out of the money of the taxpayers. The situation is different in connection with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, It was set up by the government, and those persons in Canada who pay for radio receiving licences and commercial firms who pay licence fees may be said to be the owners of that system. They are the sole contributors to it. International short wave, on the contrary, is the property of all the people, all the taxpayers; and out of the appropriation we are asking parliament to vote this year this service will be continued.

The total hours of service are approximately 141/a a day. We have different sections which we call the United Kingdom section, the Caribbean section, Australia, New Zealand and the southern Pacific, Latin America, the French section, and the European section, which takes in Czechoslovakia, Holland, Germany, Norway, Sweden and Denmark. We employ ten lan-

guages in the transmission of programs to the different countries, including English, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Dutch, German, Swedish, Danish, Norwegian and Czech. As hon. members can well imagine, if we are to transmit programs or information in ten languages, we must have people who speak those languages. They are people with special qualifications, and their fees are fairly high. Occasionally we broadcast programs in Italian, Greek, Polish and Russian.

From the opening of the international short wave service in 1945-that is when it was opened, though construction was commenced some time before-to the end of 1947, over forty thousand individual messages have been received from listeners all over the globe. In September, October, November and December of 1947 we received 8,357 letters. In January of this year alone we had 3,836 letters. It is notable that, in connection with the programs we were broadcasting to Czechoslovakia at about the time of the uprising there, we received, from September to December, some 2,522 letters. Letters have increased in number since January of this year from all countries except Czechoslovakia, where they are not now allowed to send letters to this country.

The projected expansion we have in mind for the international service is to Italy, Yugoslavia, Poland and Belgium. A careful study is being made of a possible news broadcast to Russia. The problems are, of course, the difficulty of obtaining reliable and competent personnel, and of getting reliable information with respect to listening in Russia and possible response to our service.

It might be well to bear in mind that pressure was brought to bear upon the government to build this station during the war years in order that it might be used to communicate with our men and women in the defence services in Europe. It is credited with being the finest international short-wave station in the world; certainly it is the No. 1 station of the western world. The service is very much appreciated. It is a non-revenue instrument, and on that account we ask parliament to vote this amount of money to carry on the service for another year.
